\section{Repository interface and relevant prior work\srctag{08}}
\subsection{The inspected ProveIt snapshot}
The repository was inspected at commit
\begin{center}
\texttt{4e128356d0ef75308be8ed405d89aea2ffdb8a57}.
\end{center}
The most directly relevant source is
\begin{quote}\small\ttfamily
Computability/HilbertTenthProblem/Lean/\\
Diophantine/Common/DiophantineTrace.lean.
\end{quote}
It contains the declarations \path{boundedForall_dioph},
\path{exactIter_dioph}, and \path{existsExactIter_dioph}. The first
handles bounded universal quantification; the second handles exact finite
iteration under Diophantine substitutions; the third existentially quantifies
the iteration length. Their source discharges cipher-closure hypotheses
through the \texttt{PAListCoding} infrastructure \cite{repo-trace}.

Those declarations establish Diophantineness, not the auxiliary-witness
bijections or the explicit variable counts proved here. Our construction
therefore complements them: the low-level compiler records quantitative and
multiplicity information before any global list-coding compression. This
article inspects the source; it does not independently rebuild the repository
or reproduce its axiom audit.

The combinatory-logic project provides a separate motivation. Its README
carefully distinguishes forward simulations, injectivity, different lambda
reduction conventions, and exact recursive-function equivalences
\cite{repo-cl}. We use the same discipline: a heap representation of a
rewriting system does not automatically constitute a fully abstract
translation of the repository's particular lambda semantics.

\subsection{Sorting memory histories is an established idea}
The time-order/memory-order transformation is not new. Ben-Sasson, Chiesa,
Genkin, and Tromer explicitly organize memory accesses by address and time,
then check local consistency and route between the two views
\cite{bcgt}. Their work belongs to a substantial tradition of efficient
RAM-to-constraint reductions. The later TinyRAM implementation demonstrates
this approach in a concrete verification system \cite{snark}.

Here the target is different: exact equations over $\N$, unbounded numeric
addresses, no probabilistic fingerprints, and a theorem that every arithmetic
helper is uniquely determined. A deterministic compare-exchange network is
used rather than an existential routing network whose internal routing can
have more than one realization. The distinction matters for counting zeros.

\wtag{} Within this report, Part~V prints the same address--time sorting compiler from manuscript~03 (\cref{cdc:mem:thm:memory}). Writing $L=m$ for the log length, the present counts use $2L-N$ fewer witnesses and $3N-3L-1$ more residuals, which is one \emph{fewer} residual when $L=N$; see the comparison after \cref{cdc:nh:thm:memory}.

Batcher's bitonic sorting construction supplies a simple implemented network
\cite{batcher}. Linearithmic comparator networks are also established; for
example, Goodrich gives a deterministic data-oblivious $O(N\log N)$ network
\cite{goodrich}. We use their sorting guarantees, not a claim to have improved
sorting theory.

\subsection{The multiplicity boundary}
The distinction between ordinary Diophantine representability and finite-fold
or single-fold representability is substantial. Surveys and subsequent
reduction work explicitly separate these questions \cite{ccfo2021,cco-six}.
Our results concern a family whose number of variables grows with the time
bound. Turning that family into one fixed-arity polynomial while retaining
its multiplicity would require an additional theorem; no such theorem is
assumed implicitly.

\section{Witness-faithful polynomial systems\srctag{08}}
\subsection{Source and auxiliary coordinates}
\begin{definition}\label{cdc:nh:def:faithful}
Let $R\subseteq\N^d$ be a relation. A polynomial
$P(\boldsymbol x,\boldsymbol y)\in\Z[\boldsymbol x,\boldsymbol y]$ is a
\emph{unique-extension certificate} for $R$ if, for every
$\boldsymbol x\in\N^d$,
\[
 \#\{\boldsymbol y\in\N^a:P(\boldsymbol x,\boldsymbol y)=0\}
 =\begin{cases}1,&\boldsymbol x\in R,\\0,&\boldsymbol x\notin R.
 \end{cases}
\]
A \emph{run-faithful certificate} has its complete natural zero set in
bijection with a specified set of computational runs, possibly after an
explicitly stated quotient.
\end{definition}

These notions should not be conflated. For a memory log, the source coordinates
are the log entries. For a program, most log entries become existential
coordinates constrained by the instruction semantics. Unique extension of
the memory layer then preserves, rather than collapses, the multiplicity of
source computations.

\begin{lemma}[Sum of squares]\label{cdc:nh:lem:sos}
Let $R_1,\ldots,R_e\in\Z[\boldsymbol z]$ have degree at most two. Then
\[
 P(\boldsymbol z)=\sum_{j=1}^eR_j(\boldsymbol z)^2
\]
has degree at most four, is nonnegative on $\R^{\#\boldsymbol z}$, and vanishes
exactly where every $R_j$ vanishes. At an integer assignment that violates any
residual, $P\ge1$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Each summand is a nonnegative real square. A sum of such squares is zero
exactly when all summands are zero. A nonzero integer residual has square at
least one. The degree bound follows by squaring.
\end{proof}

Nonnegativity of $P$ on all real assignments does not extend the semantic
interpretation to all real assignments. In particular, several order gadgets
below use the nonnegativity and integrality of their individual variables.

\subsection{A compact strict comparator}
Suppose $x,y\in\N$ and $x\ne y$. Introduce $b,h\in\N$ and impose
\begin{align}
 b(b-1)&=0,\label{cdc:nh:eq:compare-bool}\\
 (2b-1)(y-x)&=h+1.\label{cdc:nh:eq:compare-order}
\end{align}
\begin{lemma}\label{cdc:nh:lem:compare}
Equations \eqref{cdc:nh:eq:compare-bool}--\eqref{cdc:nh:eq:compare-order} have exactly one
natural solution:
\[
 b=\mathbf1_{x<y},\qquad h=|y-x|-1.
\]
For $x=y$ they have no natural solution.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The first equation forces $b=0$ or $b=1$. The right side of the second is
strictly positive. Thus $b=1$ is possible exactly when $y-x>0$, while $b=0$
is possible exactly when $x-y>0$. The positive difference uniquely determines
$h$. At equality the second equation would say $0=h+1$.
\end{proof}

For two records $X,Y\in\N^d$ with distinct keys $X_0,Y_0$, the same $b$ routes
every field. For $0\le f<d$, impose
\begin{align}
 L_f&=bX_f+(1-b)Y_f,\label{cdc:nh:eq:route-low}\\
 U_f&=(1-b)X_f+bY_f.\label{cdc:nh:eq:route-high}
\end{align}
There are $2+2d$ new variables and $2+2d$ quadratic residuals. The low and
high records are exact permutations of the inputs, and every new variable is
uniquely determined. A descending comparator reverses the two output wires;
it does not change these equations.

\subsection{A normalized zero test}
For a quantity $\delta$ known to be nonnegative, use $z,h\in\N$:
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:nh:eq:zero}
 z(z-1)=0,\qquad
 \delta=(1-z)(h+1),\qquad zh=0.
\end{equation}
\begin{lemma}\label{cdc:nh:lem:zero}
The unique solution is $(z,h)=(1,0)$ if $\delta=0$ and
$(z,h)=(0,\delta-1)$ if $\delta>0$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
If $z=1$, the middle equation gives $\delta=0$ and the last gives $h=0$.
If $z=0$, the middle equation gives $\delta=h+1>0$ and determines $h$.
These are all Boolean cases.
\end{proof}

The last equation is crucial. Omitting it would leave every $h\in\N$
available when $\delta=0$, creating infinitely many witnesses for the same
comparison.

\subsection{Canonical gating without cubic residuals}\label{cdc:nh:sec:gating}
A common mistake is to guard a quadratic equation $R=0$ by a selector $s$
and write $sR=0$. The residual becomes cubic. A second mistake is to leave
all private variables of a disabled instruction branch unconstrained.
Both problems admit a uniform repair.

\begin{lemma}[Canonical signed split]\label{cdc:nh:lem:split}
For every integer $r$, the equations
\[
 u-v=r,\qquad uv=0,\qquad u,v\in\N
\]
have exactly one solution: $u=\max(r,0)$ and $v=\max(-r,0)$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
If both were positive their product would be positive. Hence at least one is
zero, and their difference fixes the other. The displayed values give a
solution for all signs of $r$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Unique guarded quadratization]\label{cdc:nh:thm:gating}
Let $s\in\B$ and let $R(\boldsymbol x,\boldsymbol y)$ be an integer
polynomial of degree at most two. The implication $s=1\Rightarrow R=0$ can be
represented using two new natural variables $u,v$ and four quadratic
residuals:
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:nh:eq:gate}
 u-v-R=0,\qquad uv=0,\qquad su=0,\qquad sv=0.
\end{equation}
For fixed $(s,\boldsymbol x,\boldsymbol y)$, this representation has exactly
one extension if the implication holds and none otherwise.

For a branch with private coordinates $y_1,\ldots,y_a$, adjoining
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:nh:eq:inactive}
 (1-s)y_j=0\quad(1\le j\le a)
\end{equation}
forces all private coordinates to their canonical zero values when the
branch is disabled. If an enabled branch has unique private witnesses, the
resulting guarded branch retains that uniqueness.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The first two equations of \eqref{cdc:nh:eq:gate} uniquely split the integer value
of $R$ by \cref{cdc:nh:lem:split}. If $s=0$, the remaining two impose nothing and the
split still exists uniquely. If $s=1$, they force $u=v=0$, which is equivalent
to $R=0$. When $s=0$, \eqref{cdc:nh:eq:inactive} forces every private coordinate to
zero. Residuals in that disabled branch may evaluate to nonzero integers,
but their signed-split coordinates are still uniquely determined and satisfy
\eqref{cdc:nh:eq:gate}. Thus the construction never requires an inactive partial
operation to be defined. When $s=1$, \eqref{cdc:nh:eq:inactive} imposes nothing, and
uniqueness follows from the active branch's contract.
\end{proof}

For $B$ finite branches, select exactly one with
$s_j(s_j-1)=0$ and $\sum_js_j=1$. The labels are part of the source semantics;
if two labels describe the same observable transition, they still represent
two labelled choices unless the source explicitly identifies them.

\section{A complete memory-log compiler\srctag{08}}\label{cdc:nh:sec:memory}
\subsection{Semantics}
A source log has $m$ triples
\[
 E_t=(a_t,w_t,v_t),\qquad 0\le t<m,
\]
where $a_t,v_t\in\N$ and $w_t\in\B$. The flag $w_t=1$ denotes a write of
$v_t$ to address $a_t$; $w_t=0$ denotes a read claiming to return $v_t$.
Memory is initially zero at every address. The log is valid when each read
returns the latest preceding write to its address, or zero when none exists.
A read does not change memory.

A finite nonzero initial memory map is handled by prepending one fixed write
for every explicitly initialized address. A public, fixed order for these
writes is used. This avoids treating an arbitrary ordering of initialization
as another computational witness.

\subsection{Padding and timestamp keys}
Assume $m\ge1$, and let $N=2^{\lceil\log_2m\rceil}$. Append $N-m$ events
\[
 E_t=(0,1,0),\qquad m\le t<N.
\]
These padding writes occur after every real event. They cannot change whether
an earlier read was correct, including an earlier read from address zero.
Thus the padded log is valid exactly when the original log is valid.

For each event introduce a key coordinate $k_t$ and the residual
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:nh:eq:keys}
 k_t-Na_t-t=0.
\end{equation}
Also emit $w_t(w_t-1)=0$, retaining the trivial slot even for a constant
padding flag. The records to be sorted are
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:nh:eq:records}
 X_t=(k_t,a_t,w_t,v_t)\in\N^4.
\end{equation}

\begin{lemma}\label{cdc:nh:lem:keys}
The $N$ keys are pairwise distinct, and increasing key order is exactly
lexicographic order by address and then timestamp.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
If $Na+t=Nb+s$ with $0\le s,t<N$, then $N(a-b)=s-t$. The only multiple of
$N$ strictly between $-N$ and $N$ is zero, so $a=b$ and $s=t$. Different
events have different timestamps. If $a<b$, then
$Na+t\le Na+N-1<N(a+1)\le Nb+s$; at equal addresses the comparison reduces
to $t<s$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Deterministic sorting}
Fix a sorting network on $N$ wires with $C$ comparators. Replace each comparator
by \eqref{cdc:nh:eq:compare-bool}--\eqref{cdc:nh:eq:route-high} with $d=4$. Allocate two
comparison variables and eight output-field variables per comparator. Do not
allocate variables for unchanged wires: they retain references to their
existing coordinates.

By induction over the comparators, every record remains one of the original
records and every internal variable has a unique value. In particular, the
strict-comparison precondition remains valid. Write the final records as
\[
 (\kappa_i,A_i,W_i,V_i),\qquad 0\le i<N.
\]
They have strictly increasing keys and nondecreasing addresses.

\subsection{The adjacent-record memory test}
For the first sorted record emit
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:nh:eq:first}
 (1-W_0)V_0=0.
\end{equation}
For each $1\le i<N$, introduce $z_i,h_i,c_i\in\N$ and emit
\begin{align}
 z_i(z_i-1)&=0,\label{cdc:nh:eq:scan1}\\
 A_i-A_{i-1}-(1-z_i)(h_i+1)&=0,\label{cdc:nh:eq:scan2}\\
 z_i h_i&=0,\label{cdc:nh:eq:scan3}\\
 c_i-z_i V_{i-1}&=0,\label{cdc:nh:eq:scan4}\\
 (1-W_i)(V_i-c_i)&=0.\label{cdc:nh:eq:scan5}
\end{align}
The address gap is nonnegative, so $z_i$ uniquely indicates that the two
addresses agree. The carry $c_i$ is the preceding access value for the same
address, and is zero at the beginning of a new address group. The final
equation checks reads and imposes no restriction on a write's new value.

Why is the \emph{preceding access value} enough, rather than the preceding
\emph{write value}? Because a correct read repeats the stored value. Within
one address group, induction shows that every access value equals the stored
value immediately after that access, whether it is a read or a write.

\begin{theorem}[Exact memory certificate]\label{cdc:nh:thm:memory}
Let $m\ge1$, $N=2^{\lceil\log_2m\rceil}$, and let a fixed sorting network on
$N$ wires have $C$ comparators. The residuals above have the following
properties.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*),leftmargin=2em]
\item Each residual has total degree at most two in source and auxiliary
coordinates, with integer coefficients.
\item There are exactly $10C+4N-3$ auxiliary coordinates and
$10C+7N-4$ emitted residuals.
\item For a fixed natural source log, there is exactly one natural auxiliary
solution if the log is valid, and none if it is invalid.
\item The sum of squared residuals is a unique-extension certificate of degree
at most four, nonnegative on all real assignments.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The explicit expressions show (a). Source flags are Boolean by their
residuals. The $N$ key equations uniquely determine the keys. By
\cref{cdc:nh:lem:keys}, all comparisons are strict; \cref{cdc:nh:lem:compare} and the routing
equations then uniquely determine every comparator variable. The assumed
sorting property puts all accesses to a given address together, in time
order.

At a new group, \eqref{cdc:nh:eq:first} or \eqref{cdc:nh:eq:scan5} requires a first read to
return zero. A first write is unrestricted and establishes the group's
stored value. For subsequent records, suppose $V_{i-1}$ is the stored value
after the preceding access. If $W_i=0$, the final equation requires
$V_i=V_{i-1}$ and the read is correct. If $W_i=1$, the value $V_i$ becomes the
new stored value. This proves equivalence to memory semantics by induction
within each group. There is no interaction between different addresses.
Because padding cannot affect earlier reads, the equivalence is also valid
for the original unpadded log.

Completeness is constructive: calculate the keys, run the sorting network,
set $z_i$ and $h_i$ by \cref{cdc:nh:lem:zero}, and set $c_i=z_iV_{i-1}$. For a valid
log every residual vanishes. Conversely, any satisfying assignment has those
same keys, comparison decisions, routed fields, zero tests, and carries, so
it encodes a valid log and is unique. This proves (c).

For the count, keys contribute $N$ auxiliary coordinates, comparators
contribute $10C$, and the scan contributes $3(N-1)$. Residuals consist of $N$
key equations, $N$ flag equations, $10C$ comparator equations, one first-read
equation, and $5(N-1)$ scan equations. Hence
\begin{align*}
 A_{\rm mem}&=N+10C+3(N-1)=10C+4N-3,\\
 E_{\rm mem}&=2N+10C+1+5(N-1)=10C+7N-4.
\end{align*}
The sum-of-squares lemma proves (d).
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[The empty log]
For $m=0$ use $P=0$ with no auxiliary coordinates. The empty tuple is the
unique witness. The displayed count formulas are intended only for $m\ge1$.
\end{remark}

\paragraph{\wtag{} Comparison with Part~V.} Part~V's memory theorem (\cref{cdc:mem:thm:memory}, manuscript~03) certifies the same logs with the same sorting design. Write $L=m$ for the log length; for $L\ge1$ both use $N=2^{\lceil\log_2L\rceil}$ and any sorting network with $C$ comparators. The theorem above needs $10C+4N-3$ witnesses and $10C+7N-4$ residuals; Part~V's needs $10C+2L+3(N-1)$ and $10C+3L+4(N-1)+1$. So this compiler has $2L-N$ fewer witnesses, between $1$ and $L$: it stores keys and no shifted-address coordinate, although it also keys the padding events. It has $3N-3L-1$ more residuals, which is one fewer when $L=N$ and at least two more otherwise: its zero test has three residuals against two, and it emits constant slots for padding keys and flags. Neither theorem dominates the other, and both have the leading term $10C$. For the worked example of \cref{cdc:nh:sec:implementation} ($L=5$, $N=8$, $C=24$) the counts are $269$ witnesses and $292$ residuals here, $271$ and $284$ in Part~V. The comparators differ as well: this one is strict and has no witness at a tie, Part~V's is not (\cref{cdc:conv:b62-08}). Part~V also bounds the witness height (\cref{cdc:mem:thm:height}) and has a sort-free backend with $24L$ witnesses at a larger bit height (\cref{cdc:mem:thm:linear-memory}).

\subsection{Bounds on witness magnitude}\label{cdc:nh:sec:height}
\begin{proposition}\label{cdc:nh:prop:height}
Suppose all real source addresses are at most $A$ and source values at most
$V$. In the unique satisfying memory witness, every source or auxiliary
coordinate is at most
\[
 H=\max\{V,N(A+1),1\}.
\]
The emitted quadratic-residual coefficients have bit length $O(\log(N+2))$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Keys are at most $NA+N-1$. Comparator outputs are routed source records, so
inherit the bounds on their fields. A comparator slack is an absolute key
difference minus one. Address-gap slacks are at most $A$ and carries are
zero or a previous value. All control bits are at most one. The only growing
coefficients in the displayed memory residuals are $N$ and the timestamps
$t<N$; the remaining coefficients belong to a fixed bounded set.
\end{proof}

This is an arithmetic-coordinate bound, not a claim of constant bit cost for
an unbounded integer. An address with a million bits still has a million-bit
representation. The advantage is that one does not allocate a Boolean wire
for each address bit merely to enforce order over $\N$.

\section{Sorting costs and a restricted optimality statement\srctag{08}}
\subsection{The implemented bitonic network}
For $N=2^k$, the following fixed network is used by the code:
\begin{lstlisting}
for span in 2, 4, ..., N:
    for stride in span/2, span/4, ..., 1:
        for i in 0, ..., N-1:
            j = i xor stride
            if j > i:
                compare-exchange wires i,j
                ascending iff (i bitwise-and span) == 0
\end{lstlisting}
All bit operations here generate a finite network at compile time. They are
not operations required inside the Diophantine representation.

\begin{proposition}\label{cdc:nh:prop:bitonic}
The network sorts and contains exactly
\[
 C_{\rm bit}(N)=\frac N4 k(k+1)
\]
comparators. Consequently the explicit memory layer has
\begin{align}
 A_{\rm bit}&=\frac52Nk(k+1)+4N-3,\label{cdc:nh:eq:bitvars}\\
 E_{\rm bit}&=\frac52Nk(k+1)+7N-4.\label{cdc:nh:eq:biteqs}
\end{align}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
A bitonic merge compares opposite positions in a bitonic sequence of length
$2^j$, separates its lower and upper halves, and recursively merges both
halves. One way to see the separation is to threshold all entries at an
arbitrary value. A thresholded bitonic sequence has a single circular block
of ones. If this circular block has at most half the positions, no opposite pair
contains two ones: all minima are zero, and the maxima form a circular block
in the half-length cycle. If it has at least half the positions, no opposite
pair contains two zeros: all maxima are one, and the minima form a circular
block in the half-length cycle. Thus every entry in the lower half is at most
every entry in the upper half, and both halves remain bitonic. Induction sorts
each half. Since compare-exchange commutes with thresholding,
a nonsorted numerical output would give a nonsorted binary output at some
threshold, which is impossible. Combining an ascending sorted half and a
descending sorted half gives the bitonic input for the next merge. This is
the standard bitonic construction \cite{batcher}.

There are $j$ merge layers at stage $j$, each with $N/2$ comparators. Summing
$(N/2)j$ for $j=1,\ldots,k$ gives the stated count. Substitute that count into
\cref{cdc:nh:thm:memory}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Linearithmic existence and its exact dependency}
\begin{corollary}\label{cdc:nh:cor:linearithmic}
There is an effective family of unique-extension quartic memory certificates
using $O(m\log(m+2))$ source-plus-auxiliary coordinates and residuals.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Use an established deterministic $O(N\log N)$ sorting network
\cite{goodrich} in \cref{cdc:nh:thm:memory}. Since $N<2m$ for $m>1$, the bound follows.
\end{proof}

The archive implements the bitonic family, not Goodrich's or AKS-style
networks. The linearithmic statement is a mathematical corollary with an
explicit external dependency. It is not a benchmark result for the included
program.

\wtag{} Part~V states the same existence result with the network of Ajtai, Koml\'os and Szemer\'edi (\cref{cdc:mem:cor:optimal-size}, \cite{aks}); either established deterministic $O(N\log N)$ network gives the bound.

\begin{proposition}[Comparator-architecture lower bound]\label{cdc:nh:prop:lower}
Any binary-comparison architecture that explicitly sorts arbitrary distinct
memory keys requires at least $\lceil\log_2(N!)\rceil$ comparisons in the
worst case. Thus $O(N\log N)$ is asymptotically optimal for the
\emph{sorting stage within this architecture}.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Choose the $N$ addresses to be the numbers $1,\ldots,N$ in any input
permutation. The resulting keys have all $N!$ possible address orderings.
A binary comparison decision path has at most two successors per comparison.
Different input orderings require different sorting permutations, hence at
least $N!$ leaves. Depth is at least $\log_2(N!)=\Omega(N\log N)$. A sorting
network with $C$ comparators is a special case with at most $2^C$ comparison
outcome patterns.
\end{proof}

This is not a lower bound on all Diophantine representations, all arithmetic
circuits, or all memory certificates. A representation that does not
explicitly sort records is outside the proposition's hypotheses.

\section{Fresh names and canonical finite histories\srctag{08}}\label{cdc:nh:sec:names}
\subsection{A nominal heap model}
Let $\mathcal A$ be a countably infinite set of object names, disjoint from
scalar data. A null pointer $\bot$ is not an allocated object. An initial heap
has a specified ordered set $I=\{\iota_1,\ldots,\iota_S\}$ of objects.
Each object has a fixed finite list of typed fields: some contain pointers,
others contain tags or scalar data. A configuration also has finitely many
registers and a finite control state. Finite histories record their rule
choices, object selections, field accesses, and allocation events.

The following conventions define the precise class being studied.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(N\arabic*),leftmargin=2.8em]
\item Names can be copied, tested for equality, and followed as pointers.
Source operations cannot order names, perform arithmetic on them, or turn an
arbitrary scalar into a pointer. Rules are equivariant under permutations of
$\mathcal A$ fixing $I$.
\item Allocation returns a name never used earlier in the history, including
names of deleted objects. A finite run has only finitely many allocations.
Deletion may leave a tombstone; it does not authorize name reuse.
\item Births have a total order: time orders macrosteps, and a rule specifies
ordered birth slots within a macrostep. Rule choices and selected occurrences
remain part of the history.
\item Initially present objects and all pointer-valued inputs belong to the
specified initial structure. Subsequently appearing non-null pointers name
previously allocated objects or objects born in the current ordered slots.
\end{enumerate}
The last condition prevents an unexplained external name from acquiring a
numeric identity for free. External allocation can instead be represented by
an explicit birth event. Rules with nondeterministic selection of an existing
object are allowed; that selection is retained in the run.

A permutation acts only on names, not on scalar values, field labels, times,
rule labels, or birth-slot indices. Two histories are \emph{name-equivalent}
when a finite-support permutation fixing $I$ sends one to the other.

\subsection{The normalization theorem}
Number the initial objects $1,\ldots,S$. Number the $j$th subsequent birth
$S+j$, and encode null by $0$. Replace every occurrence of an object name in
the history by its number, including occurrences in garbage, registers,
pointer fields, selected roots, and tombstones. Scalar values are unchanged.
Write the resulting numerical history as $\NF_{\mathrm{birth}}(H)$.

\begin{theorem}[Birth-order normalization]\label{cdc:nh:thm:names}
For finite histories satisfying (N1)--(N4):
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=2.3em]
\item $\NF_{\mathrm{birth}}(H)$ is a legal history in the canonically numbered interpretation;
\item $\NF_{\mathrm{birth}}(H)=\NF_{\mathrm{birth}}(H')$ if and only if $H$ and $H'$ are name-equivalent;
\item every name-equivalence class has exactly one canonical numerical
history.
\end{enumerate}
The correspondence preserves length, rule choices, field values, and the
ordered pattern of births, accesses, and deletions.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The finitely many names occurring in $H$ are exactly initial names together
with some of its born names; counting all births also includes names that
later become unreachable. Distinct birth events have distinct names by (N2).
The map from these names to their assigned numbers is therefore injective and
preserves null and all equality tests. Apply this map to each configuration
and each transition. A fresh name remains distinct from every earlier name,
and field lookup and update commute with the map. By equivariance, each
transformed transition is legal. This proves (i).

A permutation fixing $I$ preserves the time and slot of every birth. It must
therefore preserve its birth number, so equivalent histories normalize to the
same history. Conversely, suppose the normalizations coincide. Match the
name born at slot $j$ in $H$ to the name born at slot $j$ in $H'$, fixing the
initial names. This is a bijection between two finite sets of names and sends
all name occurrences of $H$ to the corresponding occurrences of $H'$.

Such a finite partial bijection extends to a finite-support permutation of
$\mathcal A$. For completeness, regard its specified arrows as a finite
directed graph on the union of domain and range. Every vertex has at most one
specified incoming and one specified outgoing edge. Its components are cycles
and directed paths. Keep cycles and close each nontrivial path by an arrow
from its last vertex to its first; fix all remaining names. Initial fixed
points remain fixed. The resulting permutation has the required action.
This proves (ii). Existence in (iii) follows from (i), and uniqueness follows
from the deterministic numbering rule and (ii).
\end{proof}

\begin{example}[Names are not schedules]
A rule chooses to rewrite an existing object $p$ or an existing object $q$.
Even if the resulting heaps happen to be isomorphic, these are different
histories when $p$ and $q$ are distinct fixed initial objects. Likewise,
performing two independent rewrites in opposite orders normally produces two
canonical histories: birth-order normalization does not commute their time
indices. An unordered right-hand side with two indistinguishable new objects
also needs an additional quotient argument; choosing two ordered birth slots
is a semantic refinement, not a proof that the unordered quotient is solved.
\end{example}

The theorem avoids a graph-isomorphism oracle because it preserves the entire
ordered history. It does not provide canonical labeling of an arbitrary final
unrooted graph. Numerical pointer comparisons used internally by the memory
compiler are permissible: the source cannot observe them, and the compiler
has already selected a canonical representative.

\section{The local-heap compilation theorem\srctag{08}}\label{cdc:nh:sec:heap}
\subsection{A precise local instruction interface}
Fix a program $\Pi$, a record width $d\ge1$, a constant number of registers, a
maximum $r$ of births per macrostep, and a maximum $\kappa$ of scalar memory
accesses per macrostep. A macrostep is one of finitely many rule templates.
Within a template, a fixed finite sequence of primitive operations can:
read or write a field; copy a register; inspect a finite tag; test pointer
equality or nullity; select an existing object; allocate objects in ordered
slots; and update finite control. Optional scalar arithmetic must have a
fixed-size, unique-extension quadratic certificate. Addition and
multiplication over $\N$ satisfy this requirement directly.

A template has no unbounded inner loop and traverses no unbounded list in a
single macrostep. Such traversals must be decomposed into multiple macrosteps.
Different successful rule choices or selected objects count as different runs
unless the source explicitly supplies a deterministic selection convention.
An accepting or fault state is an explicit finite control state, not a
silently assumed global graph property.

For programs with deletion, give each object a live field. Allocation writes
all fields, including live $=1$, in a specified order; deletion writes live
$=0$ and changes any other fields specified by the rule. A dereference checks
that its object exists and is live. This convention admits unreachable
objects but forbids a dangling pointer from being dereferenced without a
fault transition. A program without deletion can omit the live field.

Number objects canonically as in \cref{cdc:nh:thm:names}. Field $j$ of object $p>0$
has scalar memory address
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:nh:eq:address}
  \operatorname{addr}(p,j)=dp+j,\qquad 0\leq j<d.
\end{equation}
This encoding is injective in $(p,j)$, and address $0$ is reserved for dummy
operations. It belongs to the compiler, not the pointer-only source language.
At each step the allocator counter $B_t$ is the number of objects ever born,
including the $S$ initial objects. If the selected rule creates $b_t$ objects,
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:nh:eq:allocator}
 B_0=S,\qquad B_{t+1}=B_t+b_t,\qquad
 p_{t,j}=B_t+j\quad(1\leq j\leq b_t).
\end{equation}
All $b_t$ and allocation-slot choices are forced by the selected rule.
There is no existential search for a fresh numerical name.

Each macrostep occupies exactly $\kappa$ memory slots. An unused slot is the
constant operation $(0,1,0)$; its values are not arbitrary witnesses. Fields
of the initial heap are written in a fixed order before the macrostep log.
Consequently the complete log has
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:nh:eq:log-size}
 m=dS+\kappa T
\end{equation}
events, after enlarging $d$ or $\kappa$ once to include the chosen fixed
metadata operations. Initial zero fields may still be explicitly written;
this keeps the shape uniform. A final acceptance test may inspect a bounded
number of registers or fields, which can be included in the final macrostep.

To represent acceptance within a bound, an accepting state has exactly one
padding rule: keep control, registers, and $B_t$ unchanged, and emit only
dummy operations. Padding is compulsory after the first accepting state.
An exact-length version simply omits this absorbing convention.

\subsection{Local arithmetic without hidden multiplicity}
The following construction explains the local certificate assumption in the
pointer-only case, rather than leaving it as an unspecified computability
oracle. Copies, fixed tags, addresses \eqref{cdc:nh:eq:address}, and the allocator
\eqref{cdc:nh:eq:allocator} use linear equations. A selected pointer $p$ is positive
and at most a current allocation counter $B$ exactly when there are unique
$u,v\in\N$ with
\begin{equation}\label{cdc:nh:eq:pointer-range}
  p=1+u,\qquad B=p+v.
\end{equation}
At a macrostep boundary use $B=B_t$; after reserving new birth slots, use
the corresponding updated local counter. All newborn records are initialized
before their fields are followed. A live-field read followed by equality to $1$
tests liveness. If null is an
allowed value, use the disjoint null and positive cases.

Equality tests are also canonical. Write an integer difference $x-y$ uniquely
as $u-v$ with $uv=0$, by \cref{cdc:nh:lem:split}. Apply the zero-test equations
\eqref{cdc:nh:eq:zero} to $u+v$. Its Boolean output is $1$ exactly when $x=y$.
The same construction distinguishes equal and unequal pointer values without
requiring a noncanonical witness to nonzeroness. Ordered scalar comparisons,
when included in a richer source, have the analogous signed-difference
construction.

Give the finitely many rule templates Boolean selectors $s_1,\ldots,s_q$
with $\sum_i s_i=1$. A chosen rule's ordinary equations and tests must hold;
use \cref{cdc:nh:thm:gating} to guard every degree-at-most-two equation. Force every
original template-private variable of an inactive template to zero by
\eqref{cdc:nh:eq:inactive}. The new signed-split pairs for guarded residuals are
not among these zero-clamped original variables.
Shared registers and shared event coordinates are not private variables and
are constrained by the selected template. Signed splitting of a residual
still has a unique solution when a rule is inactive. Thus there is no
assumption that an inactive partial operation was successfully evaluated.

Within the active template, primitive operations occur in a fixed acyclic
order. The source state, retained rule choice, retained object selections,
and returned read values determine its scratch variables and output registers.
Each guard helper is then uniquely determined. Halt padding has a single
selector and constant events. Because $\Pi$ is fixed, this produces only a
constant number of quadratic residuals and helpers per macrostep.

\begin{lemma}[Local certificate construction]\label{cdc:nh:lem:local}
For the finite pointer-only instruction interface above, there is an
effective fixed-size family of quadratic residual systems that checks one
macrostep. For every fixed legal step, including its selected rule, selected
objects and memory return values, it has exactly one assignment to private
arithmetic helpers. An illegal step has none. The construction extends to
additional scalar primitives with the stated unique-extension interface.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Construct the equations operation by operation as described above. The range
slacks in \eqref{cdc:nh:eq:pointer-range} are forced. Copy, arithmetic gate, and
address equations force their outputs. Signed parts and zero tests have
unique helpers by \cref{cdc:nh:lem:split,cdc:nh:lem:zero}; Boolean selectors and their guards
encode exactly the specified finite cases. The selected rule is part of the
step being checked, not an arbitrary extra witness. Inactive original template helpers
are forced to zero, and every residual's signed split is unique even in this
inactive case. Induction through the finite primitive sequence proves
existence and uniqueness for a legal step. Conversely, each zero residual
forces the corresponding primitive condition, and the selected rule's guarded
residuals force its entire sequence, proving soundness. The fixed template
size gives the size assertion.
\end{proof}

The lemma does not claim a single canonical proof of an arbitrary semantic
predicate supplied by a user. Such a predicate must be reduced to this
interface, or accompanied by its own witness-faithful certificate proof.

\subsection{A bijection, not merely a projection}\label{cdc:nh:sec:composition}
A length-$T$ run can be recorded by its finite control and registers at each
boundary, its rule choices and selected roots, its scalar event log, and its
allocation counts. Full heap snapshots are not stored. Given this record,
chronological execution reconstructs all heap snapshots, including unchanged
fields and garbage. The size of the record is $O(S+T)$ for fixed $\Pi$.

\begin{theorem}[Local heaps to one quartic polynomial]\label{cdc:nh:thm:heap}
For fixed $\Pi$ as above, a fixed well-formed initial heap $H_0$ of $S$ objects,
and $T\in\N$, one can effectively construct an integer polynomial
\[
 P_{\Pi,H_0,T}(\mathbf z)
\]
of degree at most four whose natural zero set is in bijection with the
accepting $T$-macrostep runs of $\Pi$ from $H_0$, modulo finite fresh-name
permutations fixing $H_0$. Use the stated padding convention for acceptance
within $T$ instead of at exactly $T$.

With bitonic sorting, the number of coordinates and residuals is
$O((S+T)\log^2(S+T+2))$. With an established deterministic linearithmic
sorting network it is $O((S+T)\log(S+T+2))$. The constants depend on the fixed
local program, not on $S,T$ or the names chosen during allocation.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
First normalize each nominal run by \cref{cdc:nh:thm:names}. Introduce the
$O(S+T)$ local record coordinates and helper variables from
\cref{cdc:nh:lem:local}. Fix its initial registers and control to the encoding of
$H_0$, enforce \eqref{cdc:nh:eq:allocator}, and impose the selected accepting-control
condition at the end. Keep all field accesses as common event variables.
Add the memory residual system of \cref{cdc:nh:thm:memory} for the log
\eqref{cdc:nh:eq:log-size}. These two sets of residuals share the event coordinates
but otherwise have disjoint auxiliary variables. Sum the squares of
\emph{all quadratic residuals once}. Do not square an already quartic
sum-of-squares polynomial.

For completeness, take a legal nominal run. Normalize its names and fill in
its chronological local record. Initial writes and all subsequent read/write
events are memory-valid. The local lemmas provide their unique helpers, and
\cref{cdc:nh:thm:memory} provides the memory helpers. Every residual vanishes, hence
so does the resulting polynomial.

For soundness, suppose a natural assignment makes the polynomial zero. Each
residual vanishes by \cref{cdc:nh:lem:sos}. The log is memory-valid by
\cref{cdc:nh:thm:memory}. Reconstruct the heap chronologically after its fixed
initialization writes. At a macrostep, the selected local rule is valid by
\cref{cdc:nh:lem:local}; every returned value is the value of the most recent write
to its field, or its initialized value, by the memory theorem. Updates affect
only explicitly written addresses. Thus all untouched fields retain their
values without separate frame equations. The allocator assigns distinct
ordered fresh objects, and pointer-range and live checks exclude illegal
dereferences. Induction over macrosteps reconstructs a legal canonical run.
Its final control is accepting by construction.

For the bijection, a canonical run uniquely determines its local record,
constant padding, allocator sequence and local helpers. It uniquely determines
the memory helpers as well. Conversely, the reconstruction above uniquely
determines the run from any zero. Consequently these maps are inverses.
Finally compose with the orbit bijection of \cref{cdc:nh:thm:names}. Distinct rule
choices or selected roots have distinct record coordinates, as required.

There are $O(S+T)$ local coordinates and equations, and $m=O(S+T)$ memory
events. Apply \cref{cdc:nh:prop:bitonic,cdc:nh:cor:linearithmic}. The constant-size empty-log
case is handled without a sorting network. Every residual has degree at most
two, including guarded ones, so the final degree is at most four.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Counting retained runs]\label{cdc:nh:cor:count}
Whenever the set of length-$T$ runs is finite, its number of name-equivalence
classes equals the number of natural zeros of $P_{\Pi,H_0,T}$. In particular,
a deterministic program under the fixed padding convention has either zero
or one such zero. No factor for fresh-name choices or arithmetic helper
choices occurs.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
This is the bijection in \cref{cdc:nh:thm:heap}, with cardinalities taken on its two
sides. In a deterministic run, all operational choices other than fresh
names are forced, and those names have been quotiented.
\end{proof}
For finite-tag pointer programs the set is finite because at each step there
are finitely many rules and at most $S+rT$ selectable objects. A source
primitive that nondeterministically chooses an arbitrary natural scalar may
instead have infinitely many length-$T$ runs; the bijection still holds, but
the finite counting assertion should not be applied.

\subsection{Height and numerical cost}
\begin{proposition}[Polynomial heights for finite-tag pointers]\label{cdc:nh:prop:heap-height}
For a fixed finite-tag pointer program, every coordinate of a zero constructed
in \cref{cdc:nh:thm:heap} is bounded by $(S+T+2)^{c_\Pi}$ times a program-dependent
constant. Consequently each coordinate uses $O_\Pi(\log(S+T+2))$ bits. This
claim excludes unbounded scalar arithmetic or unbounded scalar input values.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Every pointer is at most $S+rT$, every tag belongs to a fixed finite set, and
allocator counters and range slacks are $O_\Pi(S+T+1)$. Scalar field addresses
\eqref{cdc:nh:eq:address} have the same bound. There are $N=O_\Pi(S+T+1)$ padded
events, so keys and comparison slacks have quadratic bounds in $S+T+1$ by
\cref{cdc:nh:prop:height}; routed fields do not increase them. Scan variables have
at most the corresponding address or value bounds.

The local compiler adds a fixed acyclic sequence of additions,
multiplications, differences, signed parts and slack computations per
macrostep. Its depth is bounded by a constant depending on $\Pi$. Starting
from polynomially bounded local inputs, its helpers therefore have a
polynomial bound of some fixed degree $c_\Pi$. Inactive residual splitting
also has such a bound. These scratch computations do not feed an unbounded
numeric accumulator in a finite-tag pointer program. Increasing $c_\Pi$ and
the constant covers small $S,T$.
\end{proof}

This is stronger than merely knowing that witnesses exist, but it does not
make unbounded halting decidable: both the dimension and the bound depend on
$T$. Exhaustive search has a combinatorial cost even when individual integers
are small. With arbitrary scalar values the appropriate statement is the
parameterized bound of \cref{cdc:nh:prop:height}, together with the actual cost and
height growth of the chosen scalar primitives.

\section{A universal pointer-only substrate\srctag{08}}\label{cdc:nh:sec:universal}
\subsection{Two immutable linked stacks}
Use two pointer registers $L,R$, a finite control state, and a finite symbol
register. A stack cell has exactly two fields: a symbol from a fixed finite
alphabet and a next pointer. Cells are immutable after initialization. A
stack root is either null or a pointer to a previously allocated cell.

The instruction $\operatorname{push}(X,a)$ allocates a fresh cell $p$, writes
its symbol field to $a$, writes its next field to the old root $X$, and sets
$X:=p$. The instruction $\operatorname{pop}(X)$ has two disjoint cases. If
$X=\bot$, it returns an empty indication and leaves $X$ null. Otherwise it
reads the symbol and next fields of the root, returns the symbol, and sets
$X$ to the next pointer. A removed cell is retained as unreachable garbage;
no name is reused. Empty pops emit the fixed dummy slots when placed in a
fixed-shape certificate.

These operations use only finite control, pointer equality to null, field
reads and writes, and fresh allocation. Push has two real field writes;
nonempty pop has two real reads. No source operation interprets a name as an
integer. The numerical allocator and field-address arithmetic appear only in
the compiler.

\begin{theorem}[Direct Turing-machine simulation]\label{cdc:nh:thm:universal}
Finite-control programs using the two immutable linked stacks are Turing
complete. A transition of a fixed ordinary one-tape Turing machine can be
simulated with at most one allocated cell and four real scalar field
accesses, with a fixed finite amount of additional register/control work.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Let the machine's tape alphabet be $\Gamma$ with blank symbol $\square$.
Represent a tape configuration by $(q,c,L,R)$, where $q$ is the control state,
$c$ is the currently scanned symbol, $L$ contains the symbols strictly to the
left of the head in nearest-first order, and $R$ contains those strictly to
the right in nearest-first order. Missing stack elements denote blanks. It
is harmless for a finite stack to end in explicit blank symbols.

Suppose a transition reads $c$, writes $b$, changes state to $q'$, and moves
right. Push $b$ onto $L$. Pop $R$; put the returned symbol into $c$, or put
$\square$ into $c$ if the stack was empty. Set $q:=q'$. A left move is
symmetric: push $b$ onto $R$ and pop $L$. A stationary transition simply sets
$c:=b$ and $q:=q'$. Each moving transition uses one push and at most one
nonempty pop, hence at most one allocation and four field accesses.

The representation invariant holds initially by placing the finite input to
the right of the initially scanned cell into $R$ in nearest-first order and
setting $L$ null. If necessary, construct $R$ by pushes in reverse order;
this needs linear initial space. The cases above preserve the tape contents
and head position represented by the invariant, including motion into
previously unrepresented blank cells. Induction proves exact simulation of
every finite machine computation. Map halting states to the corresponding
finite-control terminal states. A universal Turing machine is a particular
finite machine, so this fixed instruction substrate is universal.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[A quartic representation for a pointer-only universal model]
For each fixed Turing machine, its input heap and time bound have the
witness-bijective quartic representation of \cref{cdc:nh:thm:heap}. Under deterministic
execution and canonical halt padding, its natural zero set is a singleton
precisely when the machine accepts within the bound, and is empty otherwise.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The simulation satisfies the local interface with fixed record width and
fixed access/birth bounds. Apply \cref{cdc:nh:thm:heap,cdc:nh:cor:count}.
\end{proof}

The constant ``four'' counts only symbol and next-field accesses in this
particular immutable-stack simulation. A general heap language that also
logs liveness, reference counts, or other metadata has different constants.
No claim is made that four is optimal.

\subsection{Why this is not a disguised arithmetic register machine}
The source cannot increment a pointer, compare two pointers by magnitude, or
factor an address. Its unbounded storage consists of allocated linked cells;
its visible data alphabet is finite. The two-stack simulation demonstrates
universality entirely at that structural level. Arithmetic is introduced
only to certify an already specified source computation. In particular,
fresh-name normalization does not assume that the source can choose the next
integer address.

The retained immutable garbage is deliberate. Removing it by a tracing
collector in one macrostep would violate bounded locality. A collector can
instead be implemented as an explicit local program, with its own steps and
invariants; name reuse after collection would additionally require the
history model to change.

\section{Local graph computation and the exact transfer boundary\srctag{08}}\label{cdc:nh:sec:graphs}
\subsection{An explicit class of graph substrates}
A finite rooted directed graph with bounded out-degree can be stored as
fixed-width object records: a finite vertex tag, a live bit if needed, and
ordered outgoing pointer fields. A local rule selects a bounded tuple of
existing roots, follows a bounded number of stored pointers, checks a finite
pattern of tags and equalities, creates a bounded number of new vertices,
and changes a bounded number of fields. Incoming edges that must be updated
must either be explicitly stored and bounded or be discovered through
separate local traversal steps. A global search for all predecessors is not
one local operation.

To give a precise simultaneous rewrite semantics, specify the order of root
roles and birth slots, read the bounded pattern before performing writes,
and either prohibit conflicting writes or specify their resolution order.
If root roles can alias, the rule must state which equalities and inequalities
are required. For a fixed bounded pattern there are only finitely many alias
patterns. A compiler can treat them as disjoint equality-test cases using
\cref{cdc:nh:lem:local}. It must not treat aliased field locations as independent.

\begin{theorem}[Bounded-local graph transfer]\label{cdc:nh:thm:graph}
For a fixed finite collection of graph rules with the interface just
described, and with globally fresh ordered births, finite accepting
occurrence histories have the quartic orbit-bijective representation of
\cref{cdc:nh:thm:heap}. The quotient fixes the initial graph identities and removes
only subsequently created vertex names. The class of such graph programs is
Turing complete.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Translate each rule into a fixed finite heap template. The bounded pattern
traversal becomes field reads; its finite tag and alias conditions become
canonical equality tests; its births and writes become allocator equations
and ordered field updates. Case splitting on the finitely many possible
alias patterns is disjoint, so it introduces no alternative arithmetic
witness for a fixed occurrence. All bounds depend only on the fixed rule.
This gives an occurrence-preserving correspondence between graph steps and
heap macrosteps, with the specified write convention. Apply
\cref{cdc:nh:thm:heap}. Two linked stacks are graphs of this form, so
\cref{cdc:nh:thm:universal} proves the last assertion.
\end{proof}

This result is independent of whether the graph is drawn in a plane, used to
represent a circuit, or interpreted as a symbolic term with shared subgraphs.
Its hypotheses concern the operational rule, not the drawing. Sharing matters:
a pointer update to a shared object is not automatically the same computation
as rewriting one copy in a fully expanded syntax tree.

\subsection{Interaction systems: an adapter, not a blanket identification}
Interaction combinators are a natural next target: Lafont's paper studies a
small universal interaction system \cite{lafont}. A bounded-port
implementation appears compatible with the interface above, but a complete
instance requires a specific syntax and implementation to be fixed. In
particular, one must prove that principal-port selection, port matching,
interface reconnection, alias cases, and creation order reproduce the chosen
source semantics. A port graph may have reciprocal-link invariants that a
plain directed heap does not automatically possess.

The theorem here applies once that bounded-local, occurrence-preserving
adapter is proved. This archive does not implement Lafont's complete rule set
or claim a checked reduction from the repository's Iota or lambda semantics
to it. The direct two-stack construction already provides a fully specified
universal instance; interaction systems are a concrete research extension,
not an unproved premise of our main result.

\subsection{A useful division of labor}
The source adapter proves \emph{which local computation is intended}. The
memory compiler proves \emph{that the recorded reads and writes fit one
chronological heap}. Birth normalization proves \emph{which name choices
should be identified}. These obligations are independent enough to be
reused separately. A correct memory trace cannot repair a wrong graph rule,
and a correct graph rule cannot repair an arithmetic certificate that accepts
a stale read.

\section{A worked certificate and executable evidence\srctag{08}}\label{cdc:nh:sec:implementation}
\subsection{Five real events, eight sorted records}
Consider the following zero-initialized memory log. A write has $w=1$ and a
read has $w=0$.
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{rrrrl}
\toprule
Time $t$ & Address $a_t$ & Flag $w_t$ & Value $v_t$ & Meaning\\
\midrule
0&7&1&4&Write $4$ to address $7$\\
1&2&0&0&Read untouched address $2$\\
2&7&0&4&Read the value written at time $0$\\
3&7&1&9&Overwrite address $7$\\
4&7&0&9&Read the new value\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
Pad with $(0,1,0)$ at times $5,6,7$. For $N=8$, the five real keys are
$56,17,58,59,60$, and the padding keys are $5,6,7$. Sorting gives:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{rrrrrrrr}
\toprule
Sorted position $i$&$\kappa_i$&$A_i$&$W_i$&$V_i$&$z_i$&$h_i$&$c_i$\\
\midrule
0&5&0&1&0&---&---&---\\
1&6&0&1&0&1&0&0\\
2&7&0&1&0&1&0&0\\
3&17&2&0&0&0&1&0\\
4&56&7&1&4&0&4&0\\
5&58&7&0&4&1&0&4\\
6&59&7&1&9&1&0&4\\
7&60&7&0&9&1&0&9\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
At position $6$, the carry is $4$ but the event is a write of $9$, so no
read-equality constraint applies. At position $7$, the carry is therefore
$9$. This illustrates why consecutive accesses, not just consecutive writes,
can be used in the scan.

The bitonic network has $C=24$ comparators. Its certificate has $15$ source
coordinates, $269$ auxiliary coordinates, and $292$ quadratic residuals.
The single quartic polynomial is specified exactly by their sum of squares.
The archive's \path{data/08-dynamic-heaps-memory_certificate.json} records every
variable, coefficient, residual and value of the unique valid witness; the
polynomial need not be expanded into a much longer monomial list.

Changing the read at time $2$ from $4$ to $5$ gives an invalid log. Its
canonical candidate assignment violates the position-$5$ read residual by
one, and the emitted sum of squares equals $1$. The theorem says more than
this particular failed candidate: \emph{no} alternative natural helper
assignment can make that invalid source log satisfy the polynomial.

\subsection{What the implementation does}
\path{code/08-dynamic-heaps-memory_quartic.py} implements sparse integer polynomials,
bitonic network generation, the complete memory residual construction,
canonical candidate-witness generation, and exact residual evaluation. Its
JSON export describes $P=\sum_jR_j^2$ through the quadratic residuals. Equal
input lengths produce the same symbolic polynomial regardless of the input
values. Source values affect the proposed assignment, not the polynomial's
coefficients or network shape.

\path{code/08-dynamic-heaps-pointer_machine.py} implements two stack heaps, their memory
logs, and birth-order normalization of action records. Its diagnostic log
omits empty-pop dummy slots; each such omission is a fixed two-slot expansion
when compiling a fixed-shape source program. The example code is not the full
local-program compiler of \cref{cdc:nh:thm:heap}, and the archive does not claim an
implemented Turing-machine frontend.

\path{code/08-dynamic-heaps-run_tests.py} compares the memory compiler with an independent
chronological dictionary simulation. It also checks sorting permutations,
small arithmetic gadgets, invalid reads, and fresh-name renamings. The seed
and exact coverage are recorded in \path{data/08-dynamic-heaps-receipt.json}.
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{p{0.69\textwidth}r}
\toprule
Check & Cases\\
\midrule
Distinct comparator inputs from $\{0,\ldots,9\}^2$&90\\
Zero-test inputs $0,\ldots,19$&20\\
Guarded residuals $s\in\B$, $R\in\{-20,\ldots,20\}$&82\\
All sorting permutations for sizes $1,2,4,8$&40,347\\
All logs of lengths $0$ through $4$ over two addresses,
two flags and two values&4,681\\
Valid logs among those exhaustive cases&1,555\\
Additional random valid logs, including 71-digit addresses&24\\
Corrupted reads rejected&80\\
Single-coordinate auxiliary increments rejected&342\\
Pairs of independently fresh-named pointer histories&12\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
Every listed check passed. The mutation count refers to increasing each
auxiliary coordinate by one in the first two random test logs, not to all
possible simultaneous mutations. Small gadget checks enumerate a finite
helper range sufficient for those input values. Their unbounded correctness
and uniqueness follow from the proofs, not from extrapolating test coverage.

The JSON verifier checks that the supplied natural assignment satisfies the
supplied residuals and that their degree is at most two. By itself it does
not authenticate an untrusted compiler's claim that those residuals encode a
particular log. That semantic link is the compiler-correctness theorem and
its future formalization obligation.

\section{Unbounded properties and two necessary obstructions\srctag{08}}\label{cdc:nh:sec:boundaries}
\subsection{Ordinary Diophantineness survives; multiplicity need not}
For the programs above, a finite run is effectively checkable. Natural
parameters can encode a program and finite input heap. Acceptance is
recursively enumerable by enumerating finite candidate runs, or by dovetailing
executions in the nondeterministic case. MRDP consequently gives an ordinary
fixed-arity Diophantine representation \cite{repo-h10}. Equivalently, once
a coded one-step relation has been proved Diophantine, the repository's exact
iteration interface provides a compositional route to finite reachability
\cite{repo-trace}.

These statements do not preserve all the additional information in
\cref{cdc:nh:thm:heap}. The polynomial there depends on $T$ in its syntax and in the
number of variables. The expression
\[
 \exists T\,\exists\mathbf z\;P_{\Pi,H_0,T}(\mathbf z)=0
\]
is a convenient description of a computably generated family, not literally
one polynomial formula: the length of $\mathbf z$ is not fixed. Encoding that
family into a fixed tuple is a separate arithmetization step.

Furthermore, a deterministic accepting run padded to different bounds
produces different bounded witnesses. Recording the first accepting time
removes this elementary duplication, but does not prove that every list
code, exponentiation representation, or compression helper has unique or
finitely many realizations. The finite-fold and single-fold literature
concerns precisely a stronger fixed-arity requirement
\cite{ccfo2021,cco-six}. This article neither assumes nor settles that
requirement.

\subsection{Finite faults versus perpetual safety}
A memory fault can be made an explicit terminal control state. The operation
``dereference null'' enters that state instead of making an unconstrained
read. For other invalid dereferences, a finite fault certificate includes the
local failing condition and the preceding valid prefix. Finite conditions
such as nullity or a tombstone read are decidable local tests.

\begin{theorem}[The existential safety boundary]\label{cdc:nh:thm:safety}
For effectively specified local heap programs, the parameterized property
``some finite execution reaches a memory fault'' is recursively enumerable
and hence Diophantine. There is a fixed deterministic finite-tag pointer
program $U$ for which the input property
\[
 \operatorname{Safe}_U(x)
 =\text{``the execution from input $x$ never faults''}
\]
is not recursively enumerable and has no existential polynomial
representation over $\N$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
A finite fault is witnessed by a finite sequence ending in a designated
fault transition. Enumerate such sequences and verify each one. This proves
recursive enumerability, and MRDP gives the first assertion. A bounded
version can instead be represented directly by \cref{cdc:nh:thm:heap}, with its
accepting state interpreted as the fault state.

For the negative assertion, choose a fixed universal Turing machine and
simulate it by the two-stack program in \cref{cdc:nh:thm:universal}. The simulation
itself performs only safe stack operations: empty pops are explicitly
handled, allocated cells are never reused, and every non-null root names an
initialized cell. Modify the simulator so that, when the simulated machine
halts, it performs one deliberate null dereference. For a natural code $x$
of a machine/input pair, the resulting fixed program $U$ never faults exactly
when the encoded machine does not halt. Malformed codes can be assigned a
fixed harmless behavior; well-formed codes suffice for the reduction.

The halting set is recursively enumerable but not decidable. To recall the
last fact, a hypothetical halting decider would let a program on input $e$
loop exactly when the decider says that program $e$ halts on input $e$, and
halt otherwise. Applying this program to its own code contradicts the
decider. If the complement of the halting set were recursively enumerable,
dovetailing its enumerator with the halting-set enumerator would decide
halting. Thus that complement is not recursively enumerable. The exact
reduction above implies the same for $\operatorname{Safe}_U$.

Finally, any set of the form $\{x:\exists\mathbf y\in\N^a,
Q(x,\mathbf y)=0\}$ for a fixed integer polynomial $Q$ is recursively
enumerable: enumerate $\mathbf y$ and evaluate $Q$ exactly. Therefore
$\operatorname{Safe}_U$ cannot have such a representation.
\end{proof}

\wtag{} In the neighbouring report \emph{liveness-beyond-halting} of this category, perpetual properties of this kind are studied systematically; the safety property above is the $\Pi^0_1$ base of its recurrence and liveness hierarchy.

This obstruction concerns an unbounded universal property, not the usefulness
of finite certificates. For a fixed bound, either a safe prefix or a faulting
prefix can be checked by finite methods. What fails is the inference from
``all finite faults have existential certificates'' to ``absence of all
future faults has an existential certificate of the same kind.'' Similar
care is required for fairness, perpetual productivity, and all-schedule
termination.

\subsection{Other limits that should remain explicit}
Our equations are interpreted over $\N$, with zero included. Replacing that
domain by arbitrary integers changes the order gadgets, and replacing it by
reals changes the discrete semantics. A standard existential domain
conversion may preserve existence without preserving uniqueness. Neither
conversion is part of the claimed bijection.

Similarly, $P\ge1$ on violated integer assignments is an exact integrality
statement, not a robustness theorem for noisy real measurements. Nearby real
points may have small residuals; an analog physical implementation would need
an additional analysis of integrality enforcement, perturbations, and energy
barriers.

\section{A formalization and integration plan\srctag{08}}\label{cdc:nh:sec:formal}
The following order isolates the genuinely new proof obligations from the
already available repository infrastructure. It is a proposed implementation
plan, not a claim that the corresponding Lean files have been created.

\subsection{Arithmetic layer}
Start with a structure for a finite list of integer quadratic residuals over
natural variable assignments. Define its sum-of-squares polynomial and prove
that evaluation is zero exactly when every residual evaluates to zero. Keep
variable allocation explicit so that counts are theorems about the syntax,
not estimates extracted from a pretty-printer.

Next prove the strict-comparator, normalized-zero and signed-split lemmas.
The comparator proof should include its precise precondition: equal keys
have no witness. Prove that routing preserves the multiset of complete
records, not merely their key sequence. A generic deterministic network
correctness theorem can then separate numerical sort correctness from the
polynomial implementation of each comparator.

\subsection{Memory semantics}
Define chronological evaluation by a finitely supported map with default
zero. The central semantic lemma should say that, after sorting distinct
address/time keys, read validity is equivalent to the adjacent-access scan.
Prove its two directions independently of polynomial syntax. Then compose it
with the comparator and scan certificates to obtain an actual equivalence of
valid logs and auxiliary zero assignments. A separate uniqueness theorem
should quantify over \emph{all} natural helper assignments, not just the
canonical witness generator's output.

The explicit formulas $10C+4N-3$ and $10C+7N-4$ can be proved by induction over
the list of comparators, then by counting scan positions. This is a useful
place to catch accidental free coordinates or unnoticed extra branch helpers.

\subsection{Names and source languages}
Represent a finite history together with its ordered allocation list. Prove
that its normalization is invariant under name permutations and reflects
orbit equivalence. The finite-partial-bijection extension in
\cref{cdc:nh:thm:names} is a small independent combinatorial lemma.

Formalize one source instance first: the immutable two-stack machine. Then
prove its local instruction certificate, its heap-log correspondence, and
its Turing simulation. Only after those foundations are checked should a
generic graph-rule frontend be generalized. The repository's combinatory
semantics should be connected by an explicit operational adapter, preserving
the chosen reduction convention rather than silently changing it.

\subsection{Interface to existing Diophantine closure}
The repository's \path{Diophantine.exactIter_dioph} and
\path{Diophantine.existsExactIter_dioph} consume a Diophantine relation on
coded natural states and Diophantine endpoint substitutions
\cite{repo-trace}. A heap frontend still needs to supply a state coding
and a theorem for its one-step relation; those are not discharged merely by
naming the closure theorem. The bounded compiler can meanwhile be developed
without committing to a global coding.

A productive API would keep two distinct interfaces: ordinary
\texttt{Dioph} for existence, and a stronger relation carrying a specified
witness equivalence and a resource-count contract. Forgetting the stronger
information should be an explicit map. That design would make it much harder
to infer single-foldness accidentally from an ordinary closure result.

\section{Further research questions and proposed topics\srctag{08}}\label{cdc:nh:sec:research}
The questions below are deliberately sharper than asking only whether
another universal substrate is Diophantine. Some seek an improved theorem;
others identify a concrete formalization or implementation target.

\begin{question}[Reduce the exact memory constant; source 08]
Can one reduce the $10C$ auxiliary and residual contribution while preserving
unique extension for arbitrary natural addresses and values? One route is to
recover an event's address from its key and the fixed range of its timestamp,
but doing so may simply move the cost into quotient/remainder helpers.
Another is to transport fewer fields and reconstruct the rest. The comparison
must count every added helper, including those of disabled branches.
\end{question}

\wtag{} Compare \cref{cdc:q:scalar}.

\begin{question}[A practical linearithmic implementation; source 08]
Implement a deterministic $O(N\log N)$ network behind the same memory
interface and determine the crossover against bitonic sorting. The asymptotic
corollary is established here using known sorting theory; a compact, verified
implementation with acceptable constants remains an engineering and
formalization target, not an open sorting-existence question.
\end{question}

\wtag{} Compare \cref{cdc:q:routing}.

\begin{question}[Certificates without explicit sorting; source 08]
Is there a unique-extension natural quadratic memory certificate with
$o(N\log N)$ total coordinates and residuals? The restricted comparison lower
bound does not exclude one. Any proposal based on products, hashing,
permutation equations or integer encodings must prove exact equality of
multisets and auxiliary uniqueness without a probabilistic soundness error.
\end{question}

\wtag{} Answered in part inside this report. Part~V's linear backend (\cref{cdc:mem:thm:linear-memory}) is a unique-extension quartic memory certificate with $24L$ witnesses and $22L+1$ residuals, with no sorting: $o(N\log N)$ coordinates and residuals are therefore achievable. Its witnesses have $O(L^2(b+\log L))$ bits (\cref{cdc:mem:thm:linear-height}). What stays open is $o(N\log N)$ coordinates with $O(b+\log L)$-bit witnesses, which is Part~V's size--height question (\cref{cdc:q:sizeheight}).

\begin{question}[Name reuse and allocation epochs; source 08]
Extend birth normalization to allocators that recycle deallocated names.
A plausible representation uses an object identity consisting of a physical
slot and a generation number. The difficulty is specifying which identity
the source can observe and preserving stale-pointer faults. A generation
encoding that changes pointer equality would not be semantics-preserving.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Unordered simultaneous allocation; source 08]
For graph rules whose newly created objects have no ordered birth slots,
construct a certificate for the true quotient rather than for an ordered
refinement. Can bounded rule automorphisms be handled by canonical local
choices without introducing global graph-isomorphism obligations? Repeated
interactions of local symmetries may prevent a purely local answer.
\end{question}

\begin{question}[Quotient independent schedules; source 08]
Birth normalization preserves scheduling. Can one additionally quotient
independent local rewrites and retain a small unique-extension certificate?
The target equivalence must specify conflicts caused by shared reads,
writes, allocation and deletion. A canonical schedule should be proved to
exist and be unique for each equivalence class, not selected by an arbitrary
existential ordering witness.
\end{question}

\wtag{} Compare \cref{cdc:q:dynamic,cdc:q:graphfront}.

\begin{question}[A complete interaction-combinator frontend; source 08]
Fix a port-level presentation of Lafont's interaction combinators and prove
the bounded-local adapter discussed in \cref{cdc:nh:sec:graphs}. Deliver the rule
interpreter, semantic simulation, polynomial compiler and tests. Explicitly
handle reciprocal ports, self-connections, parallel edges, alias patterns,
interface splicing and creation slots. This would give a particularly small
unconventional universal source with a fully exposed Diophantine compilation
path.
\end{question}

\wtag{} Compare \cref{cdc:q:graphfront}.

\begin{question}[Link to the repository's exact operational models; source 08]
Connect one of the repository's SKI or Iota reduction conventions to a
specified graph implementation. Determine whether the adapter preserves only
termination, individual reduction occurrences, or a stronger observational
semantics. Shared graph reduction and textual duplication should not be
identified without a proof of the desired equivalence.
\end{question}

\wtag{} Compare \cref{cdc:q:ski}.

\begin{question}[Canonical bounded-history compression; source 08]
Under additional restrictions, can $O(T)$ named record coordinates be
compressed into substantially fewer natural variables while preserving a
bijection? Useful restricted classes might bound address growth, recurrence
order or branching. Record the height cost and every coding helper. A
successful bounded compression is not automatically a fixed-arity
finite-fold MRDP theorem.
\end{question}

\wtag{} Compare \cref{cdc:q:compression}.

\begin{question}[Preserve counting under composition; source 08]
Develop a formal category or library of witness-bijective reductions, with
composition, disjoint sums, deterministic branching and explicitly tracked
quotients. Which existing Diophantine closure proofs can be upgraded to this
interface, and where do they necessarily lose multiplicity information?
The guarded quadratization theorem supplies one small compositional building
block.
\end{question}

\wtag{} Compare \cref{cdc:q:verified}.

\begin{question}[Verified resource and bit-height accounting; source 08]
Mechanize both syntactic counts and the polynomial-height theorem, including
coefficient sizes. Extend the latter to selected scalar primitives with
controlled growth. This would distinguish a small number of enormous integer
coordinates from an actually short binary certificate.
\end{question}

\wtag{} Compare \cref{cdc:q:verified}.

\begin{question}[Beyond exact natural semantics; source 08]
For physical or analog computational substrates, identify a finite discrete
trace relation that faithfully captures the intended computation, then
analyze what perturbation tolerance the resulting polynomial has. Exact
natural zeros alone do not establish that a laboratory system reliably
realizes the same computation. The safety obstruction also warns against
claiming existential certificates for all unbounded behavioral properties.
\end{question}

\wtag{} Compare \path{pqc:q:continuous}, the question on continuous-time and robust physical semantics in the neighbouring report \emph{probabilistic-quantum-and-continuous-computation}.

\section{Conclusion\srctag{08}}
The useful research target is not another isolated invocation of MRDP. It is
a compiler with visible operational semantics, exact arithmetic constraints,
controlled witness multiplicity, and auditable cost. For dynamic heaps, the
construction here provides that target in three separable layers: a
unique-extension memory certificate with explicit constants, canonical
birth-order names, and finite local instruction certificates.

The result is a quartic natural-zero representation in bijection with
bounded computations of a pointer-only universal substrate and its stated
local graph generalization. The implemented memory layer realizes the
explicit bitonic bound and supplies reproducible exact checks. The broader
source compiler and its Lean integration remain clearly identified proof
engineering tasks. Unbounded fixed-arity multiplicity, unordered graph
symmetries, and perpetual safety are not silently absorbed into the bounded
theorem; they mark distinct mathematical boundaries and productive research
directions.

\part{Order-free self-assembly and a positivity-restricted degree threshold}\label{cdc:part:assembly}

\paragraph{Source and scope.} \wtag{} This Part is manuscript~09, ``Order-Free Diophantine Self-Assembly and a Sharp Positivity-Restricted Degree Threshold'' (batch~62, manuscript~02; archive \path{order_free_diophantine.zip}; shipped files prefixed \path{09-order-free-}; labels \texttt{cdc:of:}). The manuscript is in three parts, printed here as three sections, with its sections demoted to subsections: (I) the degree classification for polynomials nonnegative on the real orthant (\cref{cdc:of:sec:degree}, main theorem \cref{cdc:of:thm:classification}); (II) the order-free compiler for seeded irreversible tile assembly (\cref{cdc:of:sec:assembly}, main theorem \cref{cdc:of:thm:compiler}); (III) its implementation, formalization plan, ten research questions and conclusion (\cref{cdc:of:sec:reproduction}). Its title, abstract, status statement and introduction are in \cref{cdc:sec:ms09}; the conventions of this Part are \cref{cdc:conv:b62-09}.

\paragraph{Relation to the other Parts.} \wtag{} Manuscript~09 inspected ProveIt at \texttt{4e128356d}, before this report existed, and does not cite it. Its two halves attach to different Parts. The degree classification is a fixed-arity boundary theorem of the kind collected in Part~IX: no polynomial of degree at most three that is nonnegative on the whole real orthant is a universal certificate (\cref{cdc:of:cor:no-cubic-universal}). It partly answers the question on sharp degree, arity and domain comparisons (\cref{cdc:q:degree}); see the note there. It is compatible with Part~III's depth hierarchy (flat schemes Presburger, \cref{cdc:cs:thm:flat}; separated one-counter schemes of depth~$d$ and equations of degree~$d$), whose degree-$d$ polynomials change sign on the orthant and so lie outside the classes $\Dplus_d$. The assembly compiler is a companion of Part~II's base theorem (\cref{cdc:thm:main}): both give a convex quadratic whose natural zeros are in bijection with equivalence classes of bounded executions, but here the classes are the legal orders of a monotone accretion, which are not the commutation classes of any fixed independence relation (the two-by-two example below is not the set of linear extensions of a poset). The absence of a computable spatial cutoff (\cref{cdc:of:prop:nocutoff}) is the tile case of \cref{cdc:bd:prop:nobound}.

\paragraph{Setting and hypotheses.} \wtag{} In the first half, positivity is \emph{joint}: the polynomial is nonnegative at every real point of the nonnegative orthant, inputs and witnesses together. In the second half, the tile model is the seeded, irreversible abstract Tile Assembly Model with nonnegative glue strengths, a positive temperature, a finite candidate domain supplied as compiler data, and labelled targets; the number of coordinates grows with the domain, so the compiler is not a fixed-arity representation of an unbounded predicate.
