\section{A sharp degree threshold under real-orthant nonnegativity\srctag{09}}\label{cdc:of:sec:degree}
\srcnote{\wtag{} Part~I of manuscript~09.}

\subsection{Representation classes and semilinear sets}
\label{cdc:of:sec:classes}
Throughout, \(\N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\), and every polynomial equality is an
ordinary equality over \(\Z\) or \(\R\), not an equality using truncated
natural subtraction.

\begin{definition}
For \(k\ge1\) and \(d\ge0\), let \(\Dplus_d(k)\) consist of sets
\(S\subseteq\N^k\) for which some \(m\ge0\) and
\(P\in\Z[X_1,\ldots,X_k,Y_1,\ldots,Y_m]\) satisfy
\begin{align}
\deg P&\le d,\label{cdc:of:eq:degree}\\
P(z)&\ge0\quad(z\in\R_{\ge0}^{k+m}),\label{cdc:of:eq:orthant}\\
x\in S&\iff \exists y\in\N^m\;P(x,y)=0.\label{cdc:of:eq:representation}
\end{align}
We write \(\SL(k)\) for the semilinear subsets of \(\N^k\), and
\(\CE(k)\) for the computably enumerable subsets of \(\N^k\).
\end{definition}

A \emph{linear set} has the form
\[
 b+\N v_1+\cdots+\N v_t,
 \qquad b,v_j\in\N^k;
\]
a semilinear set is a finite union of linear sets. Zero generators and
zero generators in number are allowed. The empty union is the empty set.
Coordinate projections of semilinear sets are semilinear, simply by
projecting their bases and generators. We will prove directly the
specific linear-equation facts needed below.

\begin{theorem}[Positivity-restricted degree classification]
\label{cdc:of:thm:classification}
For every \(k\ge1\),
\[
\boxed{\Dplus_2(k)=\Dplus_3(k)=\SL(k),\qquad
       \Dplus_4(k)=\CE(k).}
\]
Every semilinear set admits a \emph{single-fold} degree-two representation
in this class. Moreover, the full natural zero set of any rational polynomial of degree
at most three that is nonnegative on the real nonnegative orthant is a
finite union of natural solutions of rational affine systems. Such a
union, and hence a Presburger definition, is effectively computable.
\end{theorem}

The theorem is stronger than the observation that a globally nonnegative
polynomial cannot have odd highest degree. We allow nonnegativity only
on the orthant, where genuine cubics such as \(x^2z\) are nonnegative.
We also impose no sum-of-squares or convexity hypothesis on the cubic.

\subsection{Facewise rigidity of nonnegative cubics}
\label{cdc:of:sec:rigidity}

\begin{lemma}[Affine zero slice]
\label{cdc:of:lem:affinezero}
Let \(O\subseteq\R^r\) be an open convex set. Let \(p\) be a real
polynomial of degree at most three with \(p\ge0\) on \(O\), and suppose
\(a\in O\) and \(p(a)=0\). With \(H=\nabla^2p(a)\),
\[
 H\succeq0,\qquad \nabla p(a)=0,\qquad
 \{x\in O:p(x)=0\}=(a+\ker H)\cap O.
\]
In addition, \(p\) vanishes identically on the entire affine space
\(a+\ker H\), including points outside \(O\).
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The point \(a\) is a local minimum. More elementarily, for every direction
\(h\), the polynomial \(p(a+th)\) is nonnegative for sufficiently small
positive and negative \(t\), and has zero constant term. Its linear
coefficient is therefore zero and its quadratic coefficient is
nonnegative. Varying \(h\) gives \(\nabla p(a)=0\) and \(H\succeq0\).

Suppose first that \(b\in O\) is another zero, and put \(h=b-a\).
The univariate polynomial \(g(t)=p(a+th)\) has a zero at both \(0\)
and \(1\). Each is a local minimum because both \(a\) and \(b\) are
interior points of the region of nonnegativity. Unless \(g\) is
identically zero, each of these two distinct roots has multiplicity at
least two. That is impossible for a polynomial of degree at most three.
Consequently \(g\equiv0\), so \(h^THh=0\). A positive-semidefinite
symmetric matrix has \(h^THh=0\) exactly when \(Hh=0\).
Thus \(b-a\in\ker H\).

Conversely, let \(h\in\ker H\). Exact Taylor expansion, with no
remainder, gives
\[
 p(a+th)=t^3 C(h)
\]
for some cubic homogeneous expression \(C(h)\), since the constant,
linear, and quadratic terms vanish. Nonnegativity for small \(t\) of
both signs forces \(C(h)=0\). Hence \(p(a+th)=0\) for every real
\(t\), in particular at \(t=1\). This works for every \(h\in\ker H\),
which proves both assertions.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Why this is a special zero-set statement]
The set of all local minima of an arbitrary cubic need not itself be a
polyhedron; the spectrahedral descriptions in~\cite{ahmadi-zhang}
are more general. Here a prescribed zero level is a lower bound
\emph{throughout the chosen region}. Inside that region, every point
of the affine zero space remains at the lower bound. It is this additional
nonnegativity hypothesis that permits the stronger affine-slice conclusion.
\end{remark}

For a subset \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,r\}\), write
\[
 F_I^\circ=\{z\in\R_{\ge0}^r:z_i>0\text{ exactly when }i\in I\}.
\]
It is the relative interior of a coordinate face. Restricting a polynomial
to this face means setting all coordinates outside \(I\) to zero; its
active coordinates range over \(\R_{>0}^{I}\). The Hessian in
Lemma~\ref{cdc:of:lem:affinezero} is the Hessian of this \emph{restricted}
polynomial. The full Hessian need not be positive semidefinite at a
boundary zero: \(p(x,y)=xy\) is an elementary example.

\begin{proposition}[At most one affine zero space per face]
\label{cdc:of:prop:faces}
Let \(p\in\R[Z_1,\ldots,Z_r]\) have degree at most three and be
nonnegative on \(\R_{\ge0}^r\). For each coordinate face containing a
zero in its relative interior, choose such a point \(a^I\). There is an
affine space \(L_I\), contained in the coordinate subspace supported on
\(I\), such that
\[
 \{z\in\R_{\ge0}^r:p(z)=0\}
   =\bigcup_I\bigl(L_I\cap\R_{\ge0}^r\bigr).
\]
There are at most \(2^r\) spaces. If \(a^I\) and the coefficients of
\(p\) are rational, then \(L_I\) is defined by rational affine equations.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
For a nonempty face set
\[
 L_I=\{z:z_j=0\ (j\notin I),\quad
       H_I(a^I)(z_I-a_I^I)=0\},
\]
where \(H_I\) is the restricted Hessian. Lemma~\ref{cdc:of:lem:affinezero}
identifies the zeros in the relative interior of this face and says that
\(p\) vanishes on all of \(L_I\). Thus it is legitimate to intersect
\(L_I\) with the \emph{closed} orthant, possibly including zeros of
smaller support. Every zero is accounted for by its own support face,
and every included point is still a zero. The empty face contributes
\(\{0\}\) precisely when \(p(0)=0\). Rationality follows by evaluating
the rational Hessian at a rational point.
\end{proof}

\subsection{From affine zero spaces to semilinear arithmetic}
\label{cdc:of:sec:semilinearity}

\subsubsection{An elementary finite-generation lemma}
We use the componentwise order on \(\N^r\). Dickson's lemma says that
every subset of \(\N^r\) has only finitely many componentwise-minimal
members. A short justification is useful: every infinite sequence in
\(\N\) has an infinite nondecreasing subsequence, either by selecting an
infinitely repeated value or by recursively selecting increasing values.
Applying this successively to the \(r\) coordinates gives two distinct
terms in componentwise nondecreasing order. An infinite antichain is
therefore impossible. The minimal members of any set form an antichain.

\begin{lemma}[Natural solutions of affine systems]
\label{cdc:of:lem:linearsemilinear}
For an integer matrix \(A\) and integer vector \(b\),
\[
 V_b=\{z\in\N^r:Az=b\}
\]
is semilinear.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Let \(H=\{h\in\N^r:Ah=0\}\), a commutative additive monoid.
By Dickson's lemma, the set \(G\) of minimal nonzero elements of \(H\)
is finite. It generates \(H\): for a nonzero \(h\in H\), choose a
minimal nonzero \(g\le h\). Then \(h-g\in H\), and induction on
\(\sum_i h_i\) completes the decomposition. If \(H=\{0\}\), the
empty set of generators suffices.

Let \(M\) be the finite set of minimal elements of \(V_b\). For each
\(z\in V_b\), the finite nonempty set of solutions bounded above by
\(z\) contains a minimal member \(m\); it is also globally minimal.
Then \(z-m\in H\). Conversely \(m+h\in V_b\) whenever \(m\in M\)
and \(h\in H\). Consequently
\[
 V_b=\bigcup_{m\in M}\left(m+\sum_{g\in G}\N g\right).
\]
If \(V_b\) is empty, this is the empty union.
\end{proof}

\subsubsection{The arithmetic collapse in degree three}
\begin{theorem}[Semilinearity of the full natural zero set]
\label{cdc:of:thm:cubicsemilinear}
Suppose \(p\in\Q[Z_1,\ldots,Z_r]\), \(\deg p\le3\), and
\(p\ge0\) on \(\R_{\ge0}^r\). Then
\[
 Z_\N(p)=\{z\in\N^r:p(z)=0\}
\]
is a union of at most \(2^r\) sets of natural solutions of rational
affine systems. In particular it is semilinear.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For each support \(I\) for which there is a \emph{natural} zero of
exact support \(I\), choose one such zero \(a^I\). Unlike an arbitrary
real zero, this is rational. Define \(L_I\) as in
Proposition~\ref{cdc:of:prop:faces}. Every natural zero belongs to the space
selected for its support. Conversely the polynomial vanishes on every
selected space, so all its natural points are zeros. Hence
\[
 Z_\N(p)=\bigcup_I(L_I\cap\N^r).
\]
Each \(L_I\) has rational affine equations. Clearing denominators and
applying Lemma~\ref{cdc:of:lem:linearsemilinear} proves the result.
\end{proof}

Projecting away witness coordinates now gives
\(\Dplus_3(k)\subseteq\SL(k)\). This proof is elementary but does not
yet give a terminating procedure for selecting the \(a^I\): enumerating
natural candidates on a face with no natural zero could run forever.
The next subsection removes exactly that gap.

\subsubsection{Effectivity without assuming rational real zeros}
\label{cdc:of:sec:effective}
\begin{proposition}[Effective affine decomposition]
\label{cdc:of:prop:effective}
Given a rational polynomial of degree at most three satisfying the
orthant-nonnegativity promise, one can effectively compute a finite union
of rational affine systems whose natural solutions are exactly its zeros.
Thus natural solvability and every existential projection are effectively
reducible to Presburger arithmetic.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
For every support \(I\), use effective real-algebraic decision and
sampling to decide whether
\[
 \exists z_I>0\quad p(z_I,0)=0
\]
holds and, if so, obtain a real algebraic sample \(a^I\). These are
standard capabilities of algorithms over real closed fields; see
\cite{basu}. The empty face is checked by direct evaluation.

The Hessian equations defining \(L_I\) now have real algebraic
coefficients. Put their finitely many coefficients, including the
constant terms, in one finite algebraic extension \(K/\Q\), and choose
a \(\Q\)-basis \(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_d\). Exact arithmetic with
real algebraic numbers and such a basis is effective. For rational
unknowns \(z\), expand a typical affine equation as
\[
 \sum_j c_jz_j=c_0,
 \qquad c_j=\sum_{h=1}^d c_{jh}\theta_h,\quad c_{jh}\in\Q.
\]
It is equivalent to the \(d\) rational equations
\[
 \sum_j c_{jh}z_j=c_{0h}\qquad(1\le h\le d),
\]
by linear independence of the basis. Clear denominators, retain the
inactive-coordinate equations, and intersect with \(\N^r\).
Proposition~\ref{cdc:of:prop:faces} proves that the union so obtained is exact.
All steps terminate. The final existential affine formula is a
Presburger formula; quantifier elimination supplies an effective decision
procedure and semilinear description~\cite{ginsburg-spanier}.
\end{proof}

\begin{example}[An algebraic sample need not be rational]
The polynomial
\[
 p(x,y)=2x^3+4y^3+1-6xy
\]
is nonnegative on the orthant by the arithmetic--geometric mean inequality
applied to \(2x^3,4y^3,1\). Equality holds exactly when all three terms
are equal, so its unique nonnegative real zero is
\[
 (x,y)=(2^{-1/3},2^{-2/3}).
\]
There is no rational zero. A method that silently replaces real-algebraic
sampling by rational sampling would fail even in this two-variable case.
The field-basis step above correctly turns the affine description of this
singleton into an inconsistent system for rational unknowns.
\end{example}

\begin{remark}[What the effectiveness assertion does not say]
No polynomial-time complexity bound is asserted. The number of support
faces is exponential in the number of variables, and real-algebraic
sampling can be expensive. The orthant-nonnegativity promise itself is a
first-order real sentence and is decidable in principle, but the included
Python prototype does not implement real quantifier elimination.
\end{remark}

\subsubsection{A polyhedral extension}
\begin{corollary}[Nonnegative cubics on rational polyhedra]
\label{cdc:of:cor:polyhedron}
Let \(C\subseteq\R^r\) be a rational polyhedron, and let
\(p\in\Q[Z_1,\ldots,Z_r]\) have degree at most three and satisfy
\(p\ge0\) on \(C\). Then
\[
 \{z\in C\cap\N^r:p(z)=0\}
\]
is semilinear, with an effective Presburger definition.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Decompose \(C\) into relative interiors of its finitely many faces.
Each face has a rational affine hull and therefore admits a rational
affine parametrization. On its relative interior, the restriction of
\(p\) is nonnegative and Lemma~\ref{cdc:of:lem:affinezero} applies. For a face
containing a natural zero, choosing that zero makes the affine kernel
space rational in the original coordinates. Its intersection with the
face and the natural lattice is described by rational affine equalities
and inequalities. After clearing denominators, each non-strict inequality
is equivalent to an equality with one natural slack. The natural solution
set is semilinear by Lemma~\ref{cdc:of:lem:linearsemilinear}, followed by
projection. There are only finitely many faces.

For an effective version, compute the faces, choose real algebraic samples
where zeros exist in their relative interiors, and use the field-basis
conversion from Proposition~\ref{cdc:of:prop:effective}. The affine zero space
may be intersected with the closed face, because the polynomial vanishes
on the whole space. This avoids any difficulty with strict inequalities
at face boundaries.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Quadratic completeness for semilinearity, quartic completeness for computation}
\label{cdc:of:sec:completeness}

\subsubsection{Every semilinear set has an orthant-nonnegative quadratic}
A finite disjunction of unbounded linear sets cannot be encoded by a
bounded big-\(M\) trick without further care: the coefficients of a
selected linear set may be arbitrarily large. Nonnegative product
penalties provide a direct solution.

\begin{proposition}[An explicit quadratic for a semilinear set]
\label{cdc:of:prop:slquadratic}
Suppose
\[
 S=\bigcup_{i=1}^s\left(b_i+\sum_{j=1}^{m_i}\N v_{ij}\right)
 \subseteq\N^k.
\]
Then \(S\in\Dplus_2(k)\).
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
For \(s=0\), use the constant polynomial \(1\). Otherwise introduce
natural variables \(e_i,f_i,c_{ij}\) and define
\begin{align}
 Q(x,e,f,c)={}&\left(\sum_i e_i-1\right)^2
      +\sum_i(e_i+f_i-1)^2\notag\\
 &+\sum_{\ell=1}^k
 \left(x_\ell-\sum_i b_{i\ell}e_i
              -\sum_{i,j}v_{ij,\ell}c_{ij}\right)^2
      +\sum_{i,j}f_i c_{ij}.\label{cdc:of:eq:slquadratic}
\end{align}
Every term is nonnegative on the entire real nonnegative orthant, and
\(Q\) has degree at most two.

At a natural zero, \(\sum e_i=1\) forces exactly one selector, say
\(e_{i_0}\), to equal one; every other selector equals zero. The equations
\(e_i+f_i=1\) then give \(f_{i_0}=0\) and \(f_i=1\) for
\(i\ne i_0\). The product penalties force all inactive coefficients
\(c_{ij}\) to be zero. The remaining coordinate equations say
\(x=b_{i_0}+\sum_jc_{i_0j}v_{i_0j}\), as required.
Conversely, any expression of \(x\) in one selected linear set supplies
these variables and makes every term zero.
\end{proof}
The polynomial in~\eqref{cdc:of:eq:slquadratic} need not be convex. Its
orthant-nonnegative cross terms \(f_ic_{ij}\) are not squares. Nor is
this representation claimed to be single-fold: distinct linear-set
expressions may represent the same point.

Combining Proposition~\ref{cdc:of:prop:slquadratic} with
Theorem~\ref{cdc:of:thm:cubicsemilinear} and the inclusion
\(\Dplus_2\subseteq\Dplus_3\) proves the degree-two/degree-three
part of Theorem~\ref{cdc:of:thm:classification}.

\subsubsection{A stronger result: single-fold quadratics for every semilinear set}
\label{cdc:of:sec:singlefold}
The preceding direct union formula is economical, but its witnesses may
not be unique. Existence of a unique-witness quadratic is nevertheless
true for \emph{every} semilinear set. The key is to evaluate a
quantifier-free Presburger formula deterministically, rather than choose
one of its possible linear-set descriptions.

\begin{lemma}[An unbounded unique comparison penalty]
\label{cdc:of:lem:unboundedcompare}
For arbitrary integers \(x,y\), define
\begin{equation}
 C(x,y;p,r,c,f,h)
  =(x+p-y-r)^2+pr+(c+f-1)^2+(p-c-h)^2+fp.
 \label{cdc:of:eq:unboundedcompare}
\end{equation}
There is exactly one natural zero in the five witness coordinates.
It has \(c=\indset{x<y}\). The polynomial is quadratic and is
nonnegative whenever the five witnesses are nonnegative reals,
regardless of the real values of \(x,y\).
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Every displayed term is nonnegative on that domain. At a zero,
\(p-r=y-x\) and \(pr=0\), so
\[
 p=\max(y-x,0),\qquad r=\max(x-y,0).
\]
The equation \(c+f=1\) makes \(c,f\) complementary Boolean variables.
If \(p=0\), then \(p=c+h\) forces \(c=h=0\), and \(f=1\).
If \(p>0\), then \(fp=0\) forces \(f=0,c=1\), and
\(h=p-1\ge0\). These possibilities determine all coordinates and
satisfy all terms. Thus the zero exists uniquely, with the claimed bit.
\end{proof}

Here no big-\(M\) constant and no a priori operand bound is needed.
This is possible because \(pr\) and \(fp\) are nonnegative product
penalties, not squared bilinear residuals. Unlike the bounded affine
comparator used later for self-assembly, this penalty need not be convex.
Replacing \(x,y\) by integer affine expressions in the external inputs
preserves both the degree and orthant nonnegativity.

For a fixed modulus \(a\ge1\) and any integer affine expression
\(L(x)\), introduce natural variables \(u,v,\rho,s\) and the penalty
\begin{equation}
 E_a(L;u,v,\rho,s)
   =\bigl(L-a(u-v)-\rho\bigr)^2
        +\bigl(\rho+s-(a-1)\bigr)^2+uv.
 \label{cdc:of:eq:euclidean}
\end{equation}
At a natural zero, \(0\le\rho<a\), and Euclidean division gives the
unique quotient \(q=\lfloor L/a\rfloor\) and remainder \(\rho\).
The condition \(uv=0\) then forces
\(u=\max(q,0)\), \(v=\max(-q,0)\), and \(s=a-1-\rho\).
Thus all four coordinates are unique, including for negative \(L\).
Append \(C(0,\rho;p,r,c,f,h)\). Its complement bit \(f\) equals
one precisely when \(a\mid L\).

\begin{theorem}[Single-fold quadratic Presburger representation]
\label{cdc:of:thm:singlefoldsl}
Every semilinear set \(S\subseteq\N^k\) has a representation
\[
 x\in S\iff\exists y\in\N^m\;Q(x,y)=0
\]
by an integer polynomial of degree at most two that is jointly
nonnegative on the real nonnegative orthant, with exactly one natural
witness \(y\) for each \(x\in S\), and none for \(x\notin S\).
Such a polynomial is effectively constructible from a Presburger
formula for \(S\).
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
By Presburger quantifier elimination, obtain an equivalent
quantifier-free Boolean combination of affine order tests and congruence
tests with fixed integer moduli~\cite{ginsburg-spanier,repo-presburger}.
Strict comparisons are evaluated by~\eqref{cdc:of:eq:unboundedcompare};
non-strict comparisons reduce to strict comparisons by adding one to an
integer endpoint. Equality is the conjunction of the negations of the
two strict comparisons. Congruence is evaluated by~\eqref{cdc:of:eq:euclidean}
followed by the remainder comparison. A zero modulus, if present in the
chosen syntax, reduces to equality; a negative modulus can be replaced
by its absolute value.

Evaluate the entire Boolean circuit, including both sides of each
Boolean connective. Negation of a Boolean input \(b\) is enforced by
\((b+z-1)^2\). A conjunction \(z=b_1\wedge b_2\) is enforced by
the sum of the squares of
\[
 z+p_1-b_1,\qquad z+p_2-b_2,\qquad
 z+1-b_1-b_2-r,
\]
with natural slacks. For Boolean inputs this has exactly one natural
extension: if either input is zero, the upper equations force \(z=0\);
if both are one, the last equation forces \(z=1\). All slacks are
then fixed. Disjunction is expressible through negation and conjunction.
Constants cause no difficulty.

Sum all atom penalties and all gate penalties, and add
\((b_{\mathrm{out}}-1)^2\) for the final output bit. This is an integer
quadratic; each constituent term is either the square of an affine
expression or a product of two nonnegative witness coordinates. Hence
it is nonnegative on the whole real nonnegative orthant jointly with
the external inputs.

For any fixed natural input, each atom has exactly one natural extension,
regardless of whether that atom is true. Induction along the Boolean
circuit gives exactly one extension to all gates and their slacks.
The final output condition is satisfied exactly when the input belongs
to \(S\). Thus there is one witness for a member and no witness for a
nonmember. Evaluating both Boolean branches is essential: no inactive
branch leaves free arithmetic coordinates.
\end{proof}

\wtag{} ProveIt's Presburger development (\path{Logic/PresburgerArithmetic}) formalizes Cooper quantifier elimination over the integers and exposes a decision procedure for sentences, \path{PresburgerArithmetic.Formula.presburgerArithmetic_decidable} (a definition in \path{Lean/PresburgerArithmetic/Decision.lean}). It does not export a formula-level elimination over $\N$ in the form this proof uses; compiling such an elimination into single-fold quadratics is a formalization obligation, not an existing interface (see \cref{cdc:of:sec:formalization}).

Consequently the degree-two/degree-three classification remains valid
if representations are required to be single-fold. The single-fold
existence assertion is restricted to semilinear sets and does not
imply a single-fold representation theorem for arbitrary computably
enumerable sets. The quartic normalization below has a different
witness guarantee.

\subsubsection{Degree four retains all computably enumerable relations}
\begin{proposition}[Quartic normalization]
\label{cdc:of:prop:quartic}
Every computably enumerable subset of \(\N^k\) belongs to
\(\Dplus_4(k)\). The representing polynomial can be chosen nonnegative
on all of \(\R^{k+m}\), not just on the orthant.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
By MRDP, choose a polynomial \(F(x,y)\in\Z[x,y]\) such that
\(x\in S\) exactly when \(F(x,y)=0\) for some natural tuple \(y\)
~\cite{repo-mrdp-lean}. The usual several-input version follows from the
one-input theorem by computable tuple coding. Explicitly, the graph of
Cantor pairing is given by
\[
 2c=(a+b)(a+b+1)+2b,
\]
so finitely many pairing equations can also be included before the
following normalization.

Write \(F=F_+-F_-\) with \(F_+,F_-\) having nonnegative integer
coefficients. Compute both by acyclic arithmetic circuits using natural
constants, additions, and multiplications. Introduce a natural value for
each internal gate. An addition gate is expressed by \(z-u-v=0\),
a multiplication gate by \(z-uv=0\), and equality of the two final
outputs by an affine residual. The sum of the squares of all residuals
has degree at most four and is globally nonnegative.

Every solution of \(F=0\) extends to the unique correct set of gate
values. Conversely, in any natural zero of the sum of squares every
residual vanishes; induction along the circuit recovers its correct
values and hence \(F=0\). This proves the desired equivalence.
\end{proof}

Every existential natural polynomial zero set is computably enumerable:
enumerate its finite witness tuples and evaluate the integer polynomial.
This converse proves \(\Dplus_4(k)=\CE(k)\) and completes
Theorem~\ref{cdc:of:thm:classification}.

\begin{corollary}[Degree four is necessary even for squares]
\label{cdc:of:cor:squares}
The set \(\{n^2:n\in\N\}\) has a single-fold globally nonnegative
quartic representation, but has no representation in \(\Dplus_3(1)\).
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Use \((x-y^2)^2=0\). Its natural witness \(y\) is unique. An infinite
one-dimensional semilinear set contains an infinite arithmetic progression:
at least one of its finitely many linear components is infinite and has
a positive generator. No infinite arithmetic progression consists only
of squares. Indeed, the gaps between consecutive squares eventually
exceed its fixed positive step. Theorem~\ref{cdc:of:thm:classification}
therefore excludes degree at most three.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[No nonnegative cubic universal halting certificate]
\label{cdc:of:cor:no-cubic-universal}
No computably enumerable undecidable set has a fixed-arity representation
by a rational polynomial of degree at most three that is jointly
nonnegative on the real nonnegative orthant.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Such a set would be semilinear by the classification, and thus decidable.
\end{proof}

\subsubsection{Restrictions that must not be dropped in the statement}
The results do not decide natural solvability of arbitrary cubics, and
do not rule out any representation by a cubic that changes sign on the
real orthant. Nonnegativity only on natural assignments is a different
hypothesis and is not covered by the Hessian argument. Nonnegativity
only after fixing an input does not give the joint semilinear conclusion
unless it holds for every real nonnegative input as well. Arbitrary
variable coefficients, interpreted outside the fixed polynomial's
coordinate system, also change the question.

The quartic construction adds gate values uniquely \emph{relative to an
existing MRDP witness}. It does not make the original MRDP witnesses
unique or finite in number. Consequently neither this normalization nor
the degree threshold settles a finite-fold or single-fold MRDP conjecture.

\section{Order-free arithmetic certificates for self-assembly\srctag{09}}\label{cdc:of:sec:assembly}
\srcnote{\wtag{} Part~II of manuscript~09.}

\subsection{The seeded, irreversible model}
\label{cdc:of:sec:model}
We now give a direct compiler for a spatial substrate rather than passing
first through a Turing-machine tableau. The abstraction is mathematical:
there are no concentrations, rate constants, resource depletion,
detachment events, or finite-precision physical measurements.

\subsubsection{Tiles, bonds, seeds, and finite targets}
Let \(\mathcal T=\{1,\ldots,q\}\) be a finite palette of square tile types with
fixed orientation. Each side carries a glue label with a nonnegative
integer strength. Matching glue labels contribute their strength and
nonmatching labels contribute zero. Mismatches are permitted and give no
bond. Let \(\tau\ge1\) be the attachment threshold, or temperature.
For adjacent lattice sites \(u,v\), write
\[
 g_{uv}(b,a)\in\N
\]
for the bond contribution between a tile of type \(b\) at \(u\) and a
tile of type \(a\) at \(v\). These contributions agree on opposite
orientations as induced by the glue labels. Add a blank label \(0\), and
set \(g_{uv}(0,a)=g_{uv}(b,0)=0\).

A finite nonempty seed \(\sigma\) with support \(S\subseteq\Z^2\)
is fixed. Assume it is \(\tau\)-stable: every cut splitting its occupied
sites into two nonempty parts has total bond strength at least \(\tau\).
A singleton seed is stable vacuously. A tile of type \(a\) may be added
at an unoccupied site \(v\) when the sum of its bonds to existing
neighbors is at least \(\tau\).

\begin{lemma}[Stability and capping]
\label{cdc:of:lem:cap}
Single-tile additions of total bond strength at least \(\tau\) preserve
\(\tau\)-stability. Replacing every bond contribution \(g\) by
\(\min(g,\tau)\) leaves all attachment decisions unchanged.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
For a cut of the enlarged assembly, either both parts contain old sites,
in which case the old cut already contributes at least \(\tau\), or
one part consists only of the new tile, in which case its attachment
bonds contribute at least \(\tau\). Nonnegative additional bonds cannot
lower either sum. For capping, a sum reaching \(\tau\) either has one
term already at least \(\tau\), which stays so after capping, or has
all terms below \(\tau\), which are unchanged. A sum below \(\tau\)
has every term below \(\tau\) and is unchanged as well.
\end{proof}
From now on assume \(0\le g\le\tau\).

Let \(D\subseteq\Z^2\) be an explicitly supplied finite domain
containing \(S\), and put \(N=|D|\), \(s=|S|\). A \emph{target}
is a map \(\alpha:D\to \mathcal T\cup\{0\}\) extending the seed, with all
sites outside \(D\) blank. A target is \emph{producible} if some
sequence of legal additions produces exactly its occupied labelled
sites. Irreversibility ensures that a sequence ending in this target
never needs a tile outside it. The domain may contain holes, unused
sites, or multiple components; it is not required to be a rectangle.

\subsubsection{Monotone parallel closure}
For a fixed target, define sets of reached sites by
\begin{align}
 C_0&=S,\notag\\
 C_{r+1}&=C_r\cup
 \left\{v\in\dom\alpha:
     \sum_{u\in C_r,\ u\sim v}g_{uv}(\alpha(u),\alpha(v))\ge\tau
 \right\}.\label{cdc:of:eq:closure}
\end{align}
Here \(\dom\alpha=\{v\in D:\alpha(v)\ne0\}\).
Only the target's prescribed tile type is tested at each site.

\begin{lemma}[Sequential producibility equals full closure]
\label{cdc:of:lem:closure}
A target is producible if and only if \(\bigcup_r C_r=\dom\alpha\).
If this holds, every nonseed site first appears in a round between
\(1\) and \(N-s\).
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
If the closure is full, append each finite batch
\(C_{r+1}\setminus C_r\) in any order. Each tile was already enabled
by \(C_r\); nonnegative bonds added within the batch cannot disable it.
Thus the batches give a legal sequential construction.

Conversely, induction along any legal construction shows that all its
tiles belong to the closure. When its next tile is added, its finitely
many earlier neighbors all occur in some common closure round. It is
then added by the next closure round. If a closure round adds nothing,
all later rounds are equal, so a full finite closure has at most
\(N-s\) nonempty rounds.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Two local cuts force the unique earliest ranks}
\label{cdc:of:sec:ranks}
For a producible target, assign seed sites rank zero and each occupied
nonseed site its first-arrival round in~\eqref{cdc:of:eq:closure}; blank sites
are also assigned zero. It is not enough merely to require a site to
have enough earlier neighbors: that permits arbitrarily delayed ranks.
A second test rules out such delays.

\begin{theorem}[Two-cut characterization]
\label{cdc:of:thm:ranks}
Fix a target \(\alpha\). There is a rank assignment \(t:D\to\N\)
satisfying the following conditions if and only if \(\alpha\) is
producible. When it exists, the assignment is unique and is the
first-arrival assignment:
\begin{align}
 t_v&=0&&\text{for seed and blank sites},\label{cdc:of:eq:rankzero}\\
 1\le t_v&\le N&&\text{for occupied nonseed sites},\label{cdc:of:eq:rankbound}\\
 A_v:=\sum_{u\sim v,\ t_u<t_v}
       g_{uv}(\alpha(u),\alpha(v))&\ge\tau
       &&\text{for occupied nonseed sites},\label{cdc:of:eq:firstcut}\\
 B_v:=\sum_{u\sim v,\ t_u+1<t_v}
       g_{uv}(\alpha(u),\alpha(v))&\le\tau-1
       &&\text{for occupied nonseed sites}.\label{cdc:of:eq:secondcut}
\end{align}
Only neighbors in \(D\) matter; all others are blank.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
For first-arrival ranks, a site of rank \(r\ge1\) is enabled by
\(C_{r-1}\). Those occupied sites have ranks strictly below \(r\),
which proves~\eqref{cdc:of:eq:firstcut}. For \(r\ge2\) it was not enabled
by \(C_{r-2}\); these are exactly the occupied sites with rank plus
one strictly below \(r\). The integer support is at most \(\tau-1\).
For \(r=1\), the second sum is empty and the inequality holds since
\(\tau\ge1\). The other conditions follow from
Lemma~\ref{cdc:of:lem:closure}.

Conversely, suppose the displayed conditions hold. Define
\[
 L_r=\{v\in\dom\alpha:t_v\le r\}\qquad(r\ge0).
\]
We prove \(L_r=C_r\) by induction. At zero both equal \(S\).
Assume equality for \(r-1\), where \(r\ge1\).
If \(t_v\le r\), then either \(v\in S\), or all sites contributing
to~\eqref{cdc:of:eq:firstcut} have rank at most \(r-1\) and lie in
\(C_{r-1}\). Monotonicity shows \(v\in C_r\). Thus \(L_r\subseteq C_r\).

For the reverse inclusion take \(v\in C_r\setminus C_{r-1}\).
It has support at least \(\tau\) from \(C_{r-1}=L_{r-1}\).
If \(t_v>r\), then for each \(u\in L_{r-1}\) one has
\(t_u+1\le r<t_v\). All those support contributions occur in
\(B_v\), contradicting~\eqref{cdc:of:eq:secondcut}. Hence \(t_v\le r\),
and \(v\in L_r\).

All occupied sites have rank at most \(N\), so the closure is full.
The identities \(L_r=C_r\) also determine every rank uniquely.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[No circular activation]
An unseeded island cannot create its own justification. Its
minimum-positive-rank sites would need sufficient bonds to still earlier
occupied sites, which are absent. More generally, the theorem rejects
all self-supporting directed cycles unless they are enabled from the seed.
The earliest-rank condition is a certificate of actual reachability,
not a condition of static bond stability alone.
\end{remark}

\subsection{The explicit affine-to-quadratic compiler}
\label{cdc:of:sec:compiler}
All unknowns introduced in this section range over \(\N\). Every
constraint is affine over \(\Z\). The tile palette, threshold,
coordinates, and domain size are constants fixed before the polynomial
is constructed.

\subsubsection{Two unique-slack gadgets}
\begin{lemma}[A bounded strict comparator]
\label{cdc:of:lem:compare}
Suppose \(0\le x\le N+1\), \(0\le y\le N\), and \(M=N+2\).
The affine system
\begin{align}
 c+\bar c&=1,\notag\\
 x+1+p&=y+M\bar c,\label{cdc:of:eq:compare}\\
 y+r&=x+Mc\notag
\end{align}
has exactly one solution in \((c,\bar c,p,r)\in\N^4\). Its first
coordinate is \(c=\indset{x<y}\).
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The first equation makes \(c\) Boolean. If \(c=1\), the second
requires \(x+1\le y\), while the third has the unique slack
\(r=x+M-y\ge0\). If \(c=0\), the third requires \(y\le x\),
while the second has unique slack \(p=y+M-x-1\ge0\). The respective
bounds on \(x,y\) make both stated slack inequalities valid. The two
cases are disjoint and exhaustive, and all slacks are forced.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Boolean conjunction with unique slacks]
\label{cdc:of:lem:and}
For given Boolean inputs \(b_1,\ldots,b_k\), the affine equations
\begin{align}
 z+p_i&=b_i\qquad(1\le i\le k),\notag\\
 z+k-1&=\sum_{i=1}^k b_i+r\label{cdc:of:eq:and}
\end{align}
have exactly one natural solution in \(z,p_1,\ldots,p_k,r\), with
\(z=\prod_i b_i\).
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The upper equations give \(0\le z\le b_i\le1\).
If any input is zero, \(z=0\), and the last slack is
\(r=k-1-\sum b_i\ge0\). If every input is one, the last equation
requires \(z\ge1\), so \(z=1\) and \(r=0\). All other slacks are
\(p_i=b_i-z\), uniquely determined.
\end{proof}
This uses \(k+2\) variables and \(k+1\) equations. We will use
\(k=3\) for realized bonds and \(k=2\) for hypothetical terminality
bonds. These gadgets exploit integrality; their real relaxations need
not have the same semantics.

\subsubsection{Labels and ranks}
Introduce variables \(e_{v,a}\) for \(v\in D\) and \(0\le a\le q\),
with equations
\begin{align}
 \sum_{a=0}^q e_{v,a}&=1\qquad(v\in D),\label{cdc:of:eq:onehot}\\
 e_{v,\sigma(v)}&=1\qquad(v\in S).\label{cdc:of:eq:seed}
\end{align}
Because the variables are natural, each site has exactly one label.
Let \(\delta_v=1-e_{v,0}\) be an affine expression, not a new variable.
It is the Boolean occupancy indicator.

Introduce \(t_v,u_v\) for every site and \(h_v\) for each nonseed site:
\begin{align}
 t_v+u_v&=N\delta_v&& (v\in D),\label{cdc:of:eq:rankupperaffine}\\
 t_v&=0&&(v\in S),\label{cdc:of:eq:rankseedaffine}\\
 t_v&=\delta_v+h_v&&(v\in D\setminus S).\label{cdc:of:eq:rankloweraffine}
\end{align}
These enforce~\eqref{cdc:of:eq:rankzero}--\eqref{cdc:of:eq:rankbound}. In particular,
blank ranks and their slacks are all zero. The seed upper slack is
\(N\), uniquely determined.

\subsubsection{Neighbor comparisons and realized support}
Let \(E_D\) be the ordered neighboring pairs \((u,v)\) in \(D\)
whose destination \(v\) is not a seed site. Put \(K=|E_D|\), so
\(K\le4(N-s)\). For each such edge make two copies of the comparator:
\[
 c^0_{uv}=\indset{t_u<t_v},\qquad
 c^1_{uv}=\indset{t_u+1<t_v}.
\]
The comparator hypotheses hold because \(0\le t_u,t_v\le N\).

Let \(\mathcal J\) consist of the nonzero compatibility tuples
\[
 (u,v,b,a),\qquad (u,v)\in E_D,\quad
 1\le a,b\le q,\quad g_{uv}(b,a)>0,
\]
and write \(J=|\mathcal J|\le q^2K\). For each tuple and
\(j\in\{0,1\}\), use Lemma~\ref{cdc:of:lem:and} with three inputs to enforce
\[
 z^j_{uvba}=e_{u,b}\wedge e_{v,a}\wedge c^j_{uv}.
\]
Define the affine support expressions
\begin{align}
 A_v&=\sum_{(u,v,b,a)\in\mathcal J}g_{uv}(b,a)z^0_{uvba},\notag\\
 B_v&=\sum_{(u,v,b,a)\in\mathcal J}g_{uv}(b,a)z^1_{uvba}.
 \label{cdc:of:eq:compiledsupport}
\end{align}
No support-value variable is needed. One-hot labels ensure that for each
neighbor at most one compatibility term contributes.

For every \(v\notin S\), introduce two natural slacks
\(\lambda_v,\mu_v\), and impose
\begin{align}
 A_v&=\tau\delta_v+\lambda_v,\label{cdc:of:eq:activationlower}\\
 B_v+\mu_v&=(\tau-1)\delta_v.\label{cdc:of:eq:activationupper}
\end{align}
At an occupied site these are exactly the two threshold inequalities.
At a blank site, all bond conjunctions targeting the site are zero, so
both support expressions and both slacks are zero. There is no hidden
choice in the inactive branch.

\subsubsection{One polynomial, exact correspondence, exact counts}
Let \(L_1,\ldots,L_\ell\) be the integer affine residuals of all the
equations above, with all variables collected as \(w\). Define
\begin{equation}
 P_{\mathcal T,\sigma,D}(w)=\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}L_i(w)^2.
 \label{cdc:of:eq:assemblypoly}
\end{equation}

\begin{theorem}[Assembly-faithful convex quadratic compiler]
\label{cdc:of:thm:compiler}
The polynomial~\eqref{cdc:of:eq:assemblypoly} is a globally nonnegative convex
quadratic. Projection to the label coordinates is a bijection from its
natural zero set to the producible labelled targets in \(D\) extending
\(\sigma\). The construction uses exactly
\begin{align}
 m&=N(q+6)-3s+8K+10J\label{cdc:of:eq:varcount}\\
 \ell&=5N-s+6K+8J\label{cdc:of:eq:eqcount}
\end{align}
natural variables and affine equations, respectively. For fixed palette,
it has linear sparse description size in \(N\), without an additional
time-unrolling factor.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
A real sum of squares vanishes exactly when every residual vanishes.
At a natural zero, equations~\eqref{cdc:of:eq:onehot}--\eqref{cdc:of:eq:seed} decode
a unique target. The rank equations impose the required bounds. The
comparator and conjunction lemmas force all indicator meanings, so the
support equations are exactly those in Theorem~\ref{cdc:of:thm:ranks}.
Consequently the decoded target is producible and its rank assignment
is the unique first-arrival assignment.

Conversely, a producible target supplies its one-hot labels and
first-arrival ranks. The gadgets then give their unique values and
slacks. The two activation slacks exist by the rank theorem and are
also unique. All equations are satisfied. This proves both surjectivity
and injectivity over label assignments.

The resource ledger is
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lrr@{}}
\toprule
Block & Variables & Equations\\
\midrule
One-hot labels and seed & \(N(q+1)\) & \(N+s\)\\
Ranks and rank slacks & \(3N-s\) & \(2N\)\\
Two comparisons per ordered edge & \(8K\) & \(6K\)\\
Two three-input conjunctions per compatibility & \(10J\) & \(8J\)\\
Two threshold slacks per nonseed site & \(2(N-s)\) & \(2(N-s)\)\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
Adding these rows proves~\eqref{cdc:of:eq:varcount}--\eqref{cdc:of:eq:eqcount}.
The row system has the form \(Aw+b=0\), and
\(\nabla^2P=2A^TA\succeq0\), proving convexity.

Finally the total number of nonzero entries in the sparse affine system
is \(O(Nq+K+J)\): all gadget rows have bounded support and the support
sums contain \(O(J)\) terms in total. Since \(K\le4N\) and
\(J\le q^2K\), this is \(O(N)\) for fixed \(q\).
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Witness height and finite counting]
\label{cdc:of:cor:height}
The natural zero set of~\eqref{cdc:of:eq:assemblypoly} is finite, with at most
\((q+1)^{N-s}\) points. Every zero coordinate is
\(O(N+\tau+1)\), so a full witness has
\(O(m\log(N+\tau+2))\) bits. Counting natural zeros counts final
\emph{labelled assemblies}, not assembly orders.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
There are at most \((q+1)^{N-s}\) label assignments and at most one
zero above each. Ranks and their slacks are at most \(N\); comparator
slacks are bounded by a constant multiple of \(N+1\); Boolean-gate
slacks are at most two. Each realized support is at most \(4\tau\),
so activation slacks are bounded by \(4\tau\). These cover every
variable block.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Sparse size versus expanded size]
The stated sparse size refers to the affine rows and their sum-of-squares
presentation. Squaring a long support row can create many cross terms;
when the palette is part of the varying input, no linear-in-\(J\)
bound on the fully expanded monomial list is asserted. With a fixed
palette and bounded grid degree, each row has bounded support, and the
expanded monomial list is linear in \(N\) as well.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Terminality in the whole infinite grid}
\label{cdc:of:sec:terminality}
Checking only unoccupied sites inside \(D\) is insufficient: a target
might still grow outside the chosen domain. Checking only exterior sites
is also insufficient: an interior hole may still be fillable.

Let the exterior halo be
\[
 H_D=\{v\notin D:\text{some }u\in D\text{ is adjacent to }v\},
 \qquad h=|H_D|\le4N.
\]
Every site outside \(D\cup H_D\) has no occupied neighbor and cannot
receive a tile at positive temperature. Thus a target is terminal in
the whole grid exactly when no tile type can attach to a blank site of
\(D\) or to a site of \(H_D\).

For each \((u,v,b,a)\in\mathcal J\), add a two-input conjunction
\[
 f_{uvba}=e_{v,0}\wedge e_{u,b}.
\]
For each nonseed \(v\in D\) and each real tile type \(a\), define
\[
 W_{v,a}=\sum_{u\sim v,\ b:\,g_{uv}(b,a)>0}
                      g_{uv}(b,a)f_{uvba}
\]
and impose, with a new natural slack \(\eta_{v,a}\),
\begin{equation}
 W_{v,a}+\eta_{v,a}=(\tau-1)e_{v,0}.
 \label{cdc:of:eq:interiorterminal}
\end{equation}
For \(v\in H_D\) use the direct affine expression
\[
 W_{v,a}=\sum_{u\in D,\ u\sim v}\sum_{b=1}^q
                         g_{uv}(b,a)e_{u,b}
\]
and impose
\begin{equation}
 W_{v,a}+\eta_{v,a}=\tau-1.
 \label{cdc:of:eq:haloterminal}
\end{equation}
No halo label or rank variables are introduced.

\begin{theorem}[Terminal assembly compiler]
\label{cdc:of:thm:terminal}
Adding the terminality rows to~\eqref{cdc:of:eq:assemblypoly} gives a globally
nonnegative convex quadratic whose natural zeros are in bijection with
the producible targets in \(D\) that are terminal in the whole grid.
The exact additional resources are
\[
 \Delta m=4J+q(N-s+h),\qquad
 \Delta\ell=3J+q(N-s+h).
\]
All added witnesses are uniquely determined by the target, and the
witness-height bound of Corollary~\ref{cdc:of:cor:height} is preserved.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
At a blank interior site \(v\), each \(f_{uvba}\) equals the
neighbor-type indicator and \(W_{v,a}\) is the attachment support for
hypothetical tile type \(a\). Equation~\eqref{cdc:of:eq:interiorterminal}
is solvable exactly when it is below \(\tau\). At an occupied site,
all \(f\)'s and \(W\)'s are zero, and the equation forces its slack
to zero. Seed sites need no vacancy test. On the halo, the corresponding
statement is~\eqref{cdc:of:eq:haloterminal}. These conditions are precisely
whole-grid terminality by the preceding halo argument.

A two-input conjunction uses four variables and three equations; there
are \(J\) of them. There is one final inequality slack and equation
for each of the \(q(N-s+h)\) site/type tests. This gives the ledger.
All conjunctions and slacks are unique. Potential support at any site
is at most \(4\tau\), so the same height estimate applies.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Why the witnesses describe objects rather than histories}
\label{cdc:of:sec:examples}

\subsubsection{Feasible subassemblies form an antimatroid}
\begin{proposition}[Accessible union closure]
\label{cdc:of:prop:antimatroid}
Fix a producible target \(\alpha\), and let \(E=\dom\alpha\setminus S\).
Let \(\mathcal F\subseteq2^E\) consist of those \(X\) for which the
restriction of \(\alpha\) to \(S\cup X\) is producible. Then
\(\emptyset\in\mathcal F\), \(\mathcal F\) is union-closed, every
nonempty feasible set has a feasible one-element deletion, and
\(\bigcup\mathcal F=E\). Thus \(\mathcal F\) is an antimatroid.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The seed gives the empty set, and producibility of \(\alpha\) gives
\(E\in\mathcal F\). For accessibility, remove the last tile of a
construction of a nonempty feasible set. For union closure, first build
\(X\), then follow a construction of \(Y\), skipping sites already
present. Every tile added in the second phase has at least the neighbors
it had in the original construction of \(Y\), with the same types.
The two targets are compatible restrictions of \(\alpha\), and
nonnegative support cannot decrease. Thus \(X\cup Y\) is producible.
\end{proof}
For a nonproducible target, the same statement holds after restricting
the ground set to the sites that its closure actually reaches.

\subsubsection{A two-by-two example that is not a fixed partial order}
At temperature one, take one tile type with strength-one glue on every
side. The seed is the lower-left site \(s\) of a two-by-two square;
write \(a\) for the lower-right, \(b\) for the upper-left, and \(c\)
for the upper-right site. The full target has exactly four legal orders:
\[
 abc,\quad acb,\quad bac,\quad bca.
\]
Tile \(c\) needs either \(a\) or \(b\), not a predetermined one.
The orders \(cab,cba\) are illegal.

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[every node/.style={font=\small},x=1.65cm,y=1.35cm]
\foreach \x/\y/\lab/\rk in {0/0/s/0,1/0/a/1,0/1/b/1,1/1/c/2}{
 \draw[fill=pale,draw=accent,thick] (\x-.43,\y-.37) rectangle (\x+.43,\y+.37);
 \node at (\x,\y+.1) {\(\lab\)};
 \node at (\x,\y-.15) {rank \(\rk\)};
}
\draw[-{Stealth},accent,thick] (.45,0)--(.55,0);
\draw[-{Stealth},accent,thick] (0,.39)--(0,.61);
\draw[-{Stealth},accent,thick] (.45,1)--(.55,1);
\draw[-{Stealth},accent,thick] (1,.39)--(1,.61);
\node[align=left,text width=6.3cm] at (3.55,.5)
 {Either incoming bond enables \(c\).\\[4pt]
 Four sequential orders give one\newline first-arrival assignment and one\newline arithmetic witness.};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}

These four orders are not the linear extensions of any fixed poset on
\(\{a,b,c\}\). Every pair occurs in both possible orders among them,
so no pairwise comparison could be required by such a poset. The poset
would be an antichain and would allow all six permutations, a contradiction.
The first-arrival ranks are nevertheless uniquely \(t_a=t_b=1,t_c=2\).
Among all eight possible occupied subsets of \(\{a,b,c\}\), exactly
seven are producible; the lone impossible subset is \(\{c\}\).

\subsubsection{A capped star and genuine nondeterminism}
Place a seed at the center of a four-arm cross. Give the seed four
orientation-specific strength-one glues. For each arm provide a tile
with only its inward-facing matching glue; its other three sides are
inert. At temperature one, all sixteen subsets of the arms are
producible. The full cross is terminal in the entire grid and has
\(4!=24\) legal assembly orders. The terminal polynomial has exactly
one natural zero.

Now supply a second, distinctly labelled north-arm tile with the same
glues. There are twenty-four producible labelled partial assemblies and
two terminal full assemblies. Each full assembly still has twenty-four
orders, but the terminal polynomial has exactly two zeros. This is
intentional: the compiler does not quotient distinct physical tile labels
merely because they have identical bond behavior. It is assembly-faithful,
not unlabelled-shape-faithful.

\subsubsection{Cooperation is retained}
A temperature-two square can be arranged with a singleton lower-left
seed, two strength-two attachments leading to \(a\) and \(b\), and
strength-one bonds from both \(a,b\) to \(c\). All other exposed sides
are inert. Then \(c\) requires \emph{both} predecessors. The feasible
nonseed subsets are
\[
 \emptyset,\quad\{a\},\quad\{b\},\quad\{a,b\},\quad\{a,b,c\}.
\]
The full square has two schedules and first-arrival ranks \(1,1,2\).
The same arithmetic compiler handles this cooperative behavior without
changing its logic or choosing a causal predecessor.

\subsubsection{Negative interactions break the argument}
The nonnegativity assumption cannot be suppressed. Consider adjacent
seed sites at \((0,0),(1,0)\), with a stable positive bond between them.
Potential tiles at \((0,1),(1,1)\) each receive a strength-\(\tau\)
bond from the seed site below. Give their mutual bond strength
\(-\tau\). Both potential tiles individually attach to the seed,
so both would receive rank one in a parallel enabling test. They satisfy
the formal analogues of the two cut inequalities: each sees the seed
at rank zero, while their mutual negative bond is excluded by equal ranks.
But after either is added, the other's net support is zero; no sequential
order builds both.

Thus signed interactions invalidate the batch-serialization step and
union closure. Detachment systems and resource-sensitive chemical
networks require a different semantics and a different certificate.
Our theorem applies to nonnegative irreversible accretion, not to those
models by analogy.

\subsection{Unbounded computation and the fixed-arity obstruction}
\label{cdc:of:sec:unbounded}

\subsubsection{Marker production is computably enumerable}
Let \(n\mapsto\sigma_n\) be a computable family of finite seeds for a
fixed finite tile palette and threshold. Fix a distinguished marker tile
type, and let \(A\subseteq\N\) consist of inputs for which some finite
producible assembly contains the marker. Legal finite assembly sequences
can be enumerated effectively. At each finite stage, only finitely many
frontier sites and finitely many tile types need be tried, since
\(\tau>0\). Checking a sequence uses exact finite integer sums.
Therefore \(A\) is computably enumerable.

\begin{theorem}[From tile events to quartic Diophantine equations]
\label{cdc:of:thm:tile-mrdp}
For every such effective marker-production family, there is a fixed
finite number of natural witnesses and a globally nonnegative quartic
polynomial \(U(n,y)\) with
\[
 n\in A\iff\exists y\in\N^m\;U(n,y)=0.
\]
If \(A\) is nonsemilinear, no jointly orthant-nonnegative polynomial
of degree at most three gives such a fixed-arity representation.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Apply Proposition~\ref{cdc:of:prop:quartic} to the enumerated event set.
The obstruction is Theorem~\ref{cdc:of:thm:classification}.
\end{proof}

In a marker-universal family, the marker event is arranged to coincide
with halting of a universal computation on the seed input. Theorem
\ref{cdc:of:thm:tile-mrdp} then applies to a nonsemilinear undecidable set.
The availability of computation in seeded aTAM is established background
~\cite{doty-universal,alseth-patitz}; our theorem does not supply or
optimize a new universal tile palette. The exact implication above is
stated for any effective marker-production family, so it does not depend
on an unstated choice of simulation layout or halting marker convention.

\subsubsection{There cannot be a computable universal assembly-size bound}
\wtag{} The following proposition is the tile case of \cref{cdc:bd:prop:nobound} (Part~IX), which is stated for an arbitrary undecidable set; the proof is manuscript~09's.

\begin{proposition}[No effective complete spatial cutoff]
\label{cdc:of:prop:nocutoff}
If the marker-production event set \(A\) is undecidable, there is no
total computable \(B:\N\to\N\) such that whenever \(n\in A\), some
marker-containing assembly extending \(\sigma_n\) has at most \(B(n)\)
occupied sites.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Suppose such a bound exists. Any newly added tile has a positive bond to
some earlier tile, since the temperature is positive and all strengths
are nonnegative. Iterating this predecessor relation reaches the seed.
An assembly of at most \(B(n)\) sites therefore lies within lattice
distance \(B(n)\) of the finite seed support. This gives an effectively
computable finite region containing every relevant bounded witness.

Enumerate all labelled targets with at most \(B(n)\) sites in that
region, and test their producibility by parallel closure and whether they
contain the marker. This finite search decides \(n\in A\), contrary
to undecidability. Equivalently, the local compiler gives exact finite
integer certificates for the same bounded search, but cannot supply a
computable bound that is complete for all positive inputs.
\end{proof}

\subsubsection{Why the two polynomial degrees do not conflict}
For each \(D\), the assembly polynomial is a finite convex quadratic.
Its coefficients contain the constants \(N,\tau\), and its coordinate
list contains one block per site and neighboring compatibility. It
represents a finite set of labelled objects. Increasing \(D\) gives a
\emph{new} polynomial with more variables.

By contrast, a fixed-arity MRDP polynomial chooses its complete finite
coordinate list before all inputs and all possible execution sizes.
Theorem~\ref{cdc:of:thm:classification} says that a single orthant-nonnegative
cubic with that quantifier order can never represent a nonsemilinear set.
A family of increasingly large quadratic certificates does not contradict
this. Compressing the family must change some feature: allow higher
degree, allow sign changes, change the coefficient domain, or abandon the
fixed-arity existential-polynomial format.

There are also two distinct notions of uniqueness. The local compiler
has one full arithmetic witness for each fixed labelled target. One
halting input may have many marker-containing targets, and a fixed-arity
encoding of those targets may introduce many additional arithmetic
witnesses. Neither multiplicity is eliminated by the first-arrival theorem.

\subsection{Extensions and algorithmic consequences}
\label{cdc:of:sec:extensions}

\subsubsection{Finite graph activation}
The lattice geometry was used only to bound the number of neighbors and
to compute the finite terminality halo. On any finite graph, let vertices
have finitely many possible labels, a fixed seed set, nonnegative
label-dependent edge weights, and a positive activation threshold.
An occupied vertex may be added once, and its addition cannot diminish
support for other vertices with fixed target labels. The parallel closure,
the two-cut theorem, and the unique-slack compiler carry over verbatim.

On a graph of maximum degree \(\Delta\), replace \(K\le4(N-s)\)
by \(K\le\Delta(N-s)\), and support bounds \(4\tau\) by
\(\Delta\tau\). For fixed palette and fixed \(\Delta\), the compiler
remains linear-size. Different fixed positive thresholds at vertices can
be accommodated by using each vertex's threshold in its support equations.
This gives the same object-level arithmetic semantics for a class of
irreversible threshold-growth systems, not only square tiles.

The extension does not automatically cover arbitrary cellular automata:
a general cellular automaton overwrites states and may disable future
events. It does not automatically cover hierarchical assemblies that
attach as multi-tile units either. Those are separate transition models.

\subsubsection{A bounded-width counting corollary}
\begin{proposition}[An explicit width-dependent counting bound]
\label{cdc:of:prop:width}
Suppose the domain-neighbor graph has maximum degree \(\Delta\) and
is supplied with a tree decomposition of width \(w\) having \(O(N)\)
bags. The number of producible labelled targets can be computed in
\[
 N\,\bigl((q+1)(N+1)\bigr)^{(\Delta+1)(w+1)}
       \operatorname{poly}(q,\Delta,\log(\tau+2))
\]
arithmetic operations, up to polynomial factors for bag manipulation.
The stored counts have \(O(N\log(q+1))\) bits, so bit complexity incurs
the corresponding polynomial arithmetic factor. This
is a polynomial bound for fixed \(q,\Delta,w\), not a claim of
fixed-parameter tractability in \(w\).
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Keep only each site's label and rank as a state. There are at most
\(L=(q+1)(N+1)\) states per site. The local conditions involve a site
and its neighbors, not the auxiliary arithmetic coordinates, whose
values are forced once these states are fixed.

Enlarge each bag by adding all neighbors of its vertices. Each enlarged
bag has at most \((\Delta+1)(w+1)\) vertices and contains the full
closed neighborhood of every original vertex in that bag. The enlarged
bags still satisfy the running-intersection property. Indeed, the bags
now containing a vertex \(v\) are the union of the original bag subtree
for \(v\) and the original subtrees for its neighbors. Each neighbor's
subtree intersects that of \(v\), since an original bag covers their
edge. This union is connected.

Assign each local constraint to a bag containing its scope. Standard
bottom-up table combination over this decomposition counts satisfying
label/rank assignments, with table size at most
\(L^{(\Delta+1)(w+1)}\). One-hot semantics, rank bounds, and the two
support cuts are tested exactly. The rank theorem ensures that counting
satisfying state assignments counts assemblies, without an extra factor
for rank choices. Evaluating a support requires only bounded-degree
integer arithmetic, giving the remaining polynomial factor.
\end{proof}

For terminal counting, use the graph on \(D\cup H_D\), fixing all halo
sites blank, and include the local hypothetical-tile tests. The same
argument applies with a decomposition of that graph. No claim is made
that this elementary width bound is optimal.

\subsubsection{Boolean observables and shape projections}
A specified marker at a fixed site can be required by fixing its label
indicator. A fixed finite Boolean circuit on site-label bits can be
encoded with unique affine Boolean gates and slacks, preserving one
arithmetic extension per assembly. This is useful for accepting a
particular output pattern or requiring a prescribed set of sites to be
occupied.

Projection from labelled assemblies to unlabelled supports can merge
solutions. The two-north-tile star is already a counterexample to
shape-faithfulness. A separate canonical labelling selection would be
needed to obtain one witness per shape, and such a selection is not
supplied by simply dropping label coordinates from the statement.

\section{Reproduction, formalization, and further research\srctag{09}}\label{cdc:of:sec:reproduction}
\srcnote{\wtag{} Part~III of manuscript~09.}

\subsection{Executable compiler and exact finite checks}
\label{cdc:of:sec:verification}

\subsubsection{What the package implements}
The standard-library Python module \path{code/09-order-free-assembly_compiler.py}
constructs the literal affine rows of the base and terminal compilers.
Rows are stored as sparse integer coefficient maps plus a constant.
The polynomial is specified exactly as their sum of squares, so no
symbolic expansion is required. The module also contains a canonical
witness constructor, an arithmetic row checker, and a JSON exporter.

Two separate finite dynamics implementations are used: a parallel-closure
routine computes arrival ranks, while an asynchronous search enumerates
all reachable labelled states by legal single-tile additions. Their
agreement is tested for every seed-extending labelling in four fixtures.
The exported certificate checker evaluates the saved rows and witness;
it does not call the compiler or reconstruct a dynamics trace.

The implementation checks basic palette, threshold, and seed-label
validity. General multi-site seed stability is a mathematical precondition,
not a property automatically proved by the prototype. All four executable
fixtures use singleton seeds and meet it vacuously.

\subsubsection{Results of the reproduced tests}
Running \path{code/09-order-free-verify.py} produced the following exact counts:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lrrrr@{}}
\toprule
Fixture & Labelings & Producible & Terminal & Full-target orders\\
\midrule
Two-by-two diamond & 8 & 7 & 0 & 4\\
Capped four-arm star & 1296 & 16 & 1 & 24\\
Star with two north labels & 2401 & 24 & 2 & 24\\
Cooperative square & 125 & 5 & 1 & 2\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
The diamond has no whole-grid terminal assembly in this domain because
its exposed strength-one glues permit growth beyond the domain. The
capped fixtures correctly remove that possibility. All labelings counted
in the second column extend the seed, including many impossible
assignments of tile types to other sites.

The exact base and terminal resource counts are:
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}lrrrrrr@{}}
\toprule
Fixture & \(K\) & \(J\) & Base \(m\) & Base \(\ell\) & Terminal \(m\) & Terminal \(\ell\)\\
\midrule
Diamond & 6 & 6 & 133 & 103 & 168 & 132\\
Capped star & 4 & 8 & 164 & 112 & 256 & 196\\
Alternative star & 4 & 10 & 189 & 128 & 301 & 230\\
Cooperative square & 6 & 12 & 205 & 151 & 297 & 231\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
Here the compatibility count \(J\) includes every nonzero type pair on
an eligible oriented edge, even if a particular pair cannot occur in a
producible target. This explains why it can exceed the number of bonds
in the illustrated full assembly.

Additional exact checks covered 568 comparator input cases, all 12
Boolean input cases for the two- and three-input conjunctions, and 3,882
rank assignments across all producible targets of the fixtures. Each
producible target admitted precisely its canonical rank assignment.
A separate exhaustive test of all 125 relevant rank assignments for
all eight diamond targets also checked the rejected isolated tile.
All 1,304 tested natural single-coordinate perturbations of the four
exported witnesses were rejected by at least one arithmetic row.

For the positivity constructions, the test suite evaluated 512 natural
grid points of \((x-y)^2(1+z)\) and 476,656 assignments to the explicit
quadratic for \(2\N\cup(1+3\N)\), confirming its projected behavior
for inputs from zero to thirty. These checks are illustrations and
implementation tests. The universal cubic classification rests on the
proofs in \cref{cdc:of:sec:degree}, not on these finite experiments.

\subsubsection{Reproduction commands and trust boundary}
From the extracted package directory:
\begin{verbatim}
python code/verify.py
pdflatex -interaction=nonstopmode -halt-on-error order_free_diophantine.tex
pdflatex -interaction=nonstopmode -halt-on-error order_free_diophantine.tex
\end{verbatim}
\srcnote{\wtag{} This command listing is the manuscript's own and keeps its delivered layout, in which the programs import one another by their delivered names; the shipped copies carry the prefix \path{09-order-free-} and must be copied back to that layout, outside the collection, before they are run. Where \texttt{python} does not resolve, use \texttt{py}. The README of this report gives rerun recipes that write only into the copy. The manuscript's own \texttt{article.tex} is not shipped; its text is this Part.}
The additional module \path{code/09-order-free-presburger_gadgets.py} implements the
unbounded comparison and signed-divisibility penalties. The tests check
uniqueness for 121 signed comparison operand pairs and 186 signed-operand,
positive-modulus pairs. This is a gadget library, not an implementation
of full Presburger quantifier elimination.

The test script writes \path{data/09-order-free-verification_report.json} and four
literal certificate files (shipped as \path{data/09-order-free-*_certificate.json}). The JSON format stores the integer rows,
variable names, input tile system, selected target, and witness. A row
has semantics
\[
 \texttt{constant}+\sum_{(i,c)\in\texttt{terms}}c\,w_i=0.
\]
The prototype verifies these identities with exact Python integers.
It is not an SMT proof, a Lean proof, or a proof that the source compiler
is free of all defects. The mathematical proof establishes general
soundness and completeness; the finite tests exercise its implementation
and edge cases.

\subsection{A concrete route into the repository's formal development}
\label{cdc:of:sec:formalization}
No new Lean file in this package is labelled as verified. The following
is an implementation plan with explicit proof obligations, not a claim
that those obligations are already discharged.

\subsubsection{The low-degree classification}
The most self-contained starting point is the affine-zero lemma. A
formal proof can avoid general multivariate Taylor analysis by expanding
\(p(a+th)\) as a univariate polynomial of degree at most three. One
then proves the small-positive-and-negative sign lemmas, the double-root
argument, and the positive-semidefinite kernel equivalence. Restricting
variables to a coordinate face is a polynomial substitution.

The elementary natural-zero decomposition can use a finite choice of
one natural zero per occupied support face. Formalizing the
semilinearity of \(Az=b\) requires the finite minimal-element theorem
for \(\N^r\) and the monoid decomposition in
Lemma~\ref{cdc:of:lem:linearsemilinear}. The constructive quadratic
\eqref{cdc:of:eq:slquadratic} then reduces to elementary arithmetic and
nonnegativity. For the stronger single-fold theorem, formalize the
unbounded comparison and signed Euclidean-division penalties, then
compose them with the existing Presburger quantifier eliminator and a
unique Boolean-circuit evaluator. This gives the mathematical classification without first
formalizing a real-algebraic sampling engine.

The effective strengthening is a separate development. It needs certified
algebraic samples and a certified number-field basis conversion before
feeding a Presburger formula to the existing decision procedure
~\cite{repo-presburger}. Treating sampling as an unproved oracle would
not establish an unconditional executable decision theorem.

\subsubsection{The assembly compiler}
A finite graph formulation is preferable as the core abstraction. Define
finite labels, support sums, monotone closure, sequential additions, and
first-arrival ranks. Prove Lemma~\ref{cdc:of:lem:closure} and
Theorem~\ref{cdc:of:thm:ranks} before introducing any polynomial syntax.
Then formalize each unique-slack gadget and establish that the generated
finite list of affine equations is equivalent to the semantic rank
conditions. Sum-of-squares reflection supplies the final polynomial.

The principal endpoint should be a bijection, not merely an existential
soundness theorem. Its inverse is the canonical witness constructor.
This permits exact counting theorems to be transported without another
uniqueness proof. The terminal extension should explicitly quantify over
the interior blanks and one exterior neighbor halo.

\subsubsection{The MRDP bridge and its limits}
The repository's \code{Diophantine.mrdp} already has the required
fixed-finite-witness shape~\cite{repo-mrdp-lean}. To use it for marker
production, the remaining obligation is to prove the chosen encoded
event predicate recursively enumerable. The bridge does not require
claiming that this article's explicit spatial compiler itself has
fixed arity.

A circuit-to-quartic normalization can be proved once as a general library
construction on polynomials, independently of tile semantics. Its theorem
should state unique extension only for gate variables given the original
input and witness. That wording prevents an accidental strengthening to
single-fold MRDP.

\subsection{Further research questions and proposed projects}
\label{cdc:of:sec:questions}
The following questions arise directly from the proved statements.
They are proposed problems; their being listed here is not a claim that
all are previously unstudied.

\begin{question}[Single-fold representations of semilinear sets; source 09]
Theorem~\ref{cdc:of:thm:singlefoldsl} settles existence of a single-fold
orthant-nonnegative quadratic. What are the optimal witness-dimension
and coefficient-height bounds in terms of a semilinear presentation or
an already quantifier-free Presburger formula? How large an improvement
is possible over one unique-evaluation block per atom and Boolean gate?
\end{question}
One alternative to deterministic formula evaluation is a disjoint
canonical decomposition into linear pieces with uniquely representable
generator coefficients. Comparing the dimension costs of these routes
could yield sharper arithmetic certificates than the general construction.

\begin{question}[Effective cubic decomposition without full real quantifier elimination; source 09]
Can the facewise affine zero spaces be recovered by a simpler exact
algorithm using the special geometry of cubics, perhaps the
semidefinite descriptions of~\cite{ahmadi-zhang}, followed by rational
linear algebra? Can one bound the bit complexity of the resulting
Presburger presentation in useful restricted classes?
\end{question}
The cubic classification already proves decidability; the unresolved
algorithmic target is a practical certified reduction. Exact feasibility
and algebraic sampling must remain distinct from numerical
semidefinite optimization.

\begin{question}[Sharp positivity hypotheses; source 09]
How far can full real-orthant nonnegativity be weakened while preserving
semilinearity of cubic natural zero sets? What happens under a finite
collection of rational-polyhedral positivity promises, or positivity
only on natural assignments, or positivity on nonlinear semialgebraic regions?
\end{question}
The finite-polyhedral version follows by applying
Corollary~\ref{cdc:of:cor:polyhedron} to each piece. More general promises need
care: a proof that uses local minima must still justify a neighborhood
of nonnegativity around every relevant point within its face.

\begin{question}[Fewer variables in the order-free compiler; source 09]
Can the two comparisons per edge and the two three-input conjunctions
per compatibility be shared or replaced to reduce the exact coefficients
in~\eqref{cdc:of:eq:varcount}, while preserving convexity and unique witnesses?
Can a lower bound distinguish one-rank-per-site encodings from explicit
round-by-round encodings?
\end{question}
The present ledger is explicit and validated, but not advertised as
optimal. Any optimization should retain a local uniqueness theorem for
every replacement gadget and should count all slacks.

\begin{question}[Canonical certificates for hierarchical self-assembly; source 09]
Can a producible hierarchical assembly be assigned a canonical,
polynomial-size arithmetic certificate that does not enumerate all
possible binary merge trees? Is there a counterpart of earliest ranks
whose local conditions enforce a unique hierarchy?
\end{question}
Doty's greedy producibility results~\cite{doty-hierarchical} are a
natural starting point. The obstruction is that merges combine objects,
not single sites, so the two-cut theorem is not immediately applicable.

\begin{question}[Negative glues and reversible growth; source 09]
Which signed or reversible systems still admit an efficiently computable
canonical witness of their final object? Can a restricted dependency
condition restore serializability of parallel layers?
\end{question}
The two-tile signed example proves that unrestricted negative bonds do
not permit a naive extension. A useful result would isolate exact
semantic conditions under which batches remain serializable, rather
than merely adding signed terms to the support polynomial.

\wtag{} Compare \cref{cdc:q:dynamic}.

\begin{question}[Shape-faithful rather than label-faithful witnesses; source 09]
For nondeterministic tile systems, can one choose a canonical producible
labelling of each attainable shape using a polynomial-size direct
certificate? What is the counting complexity of this quotient problem
for natural restricted tile families?
\end{question}
First-arrival ranks remove schedule multiplicity, not label
multiplicity. The alternative-star fixture provides a small regression
test for any proposed quotient construction.

\begin{question}[Width dependence and arithmetic compression; source 09]
Can the counting bound in Proposition~\ref{cdc:of:prop:width} be made
fixed-parameter tractable in treewidth, avoiding the factor
\(N^{O(w)}\) caused by ranks? Are only relative rank orders and a bounded
amount of threshold information needed at a separator?
\end{question}
A compressed boundary state must preserve both support at the preceding
round and non-support one round earlier. Losing that second distinction
would count delayed rank assignments again.

\wtag{} Compare \cref{cdc:q:counting}.

\begin{question}[Fixed-arity assembly-faithful encodings; source 09]
Can finite labelled assemblies and their earliest ranks be encoded into
a fixed tuple of integers, with explicit Diophantine decoding that
retains a controlled number of arithmetic witnesses? Which parts can be
made single-fold without assuming a general finite-fold MRDP result?
\end{question}
Theorem~\ref{cdc:of:thm:classification} excludes jointly orthant-nonnegative
cubics for any nonsemilinear unbounded event. A successful construction
must therefore respect this degree obstruction. The distinction between
unique object coding and unique witnesses for arithmetic relations such
as exponentiation must be tracked explicitly.

\wtag{} Compare \cref{cdc:q:compression}.

\begin{question}[A minimal verified vertical slice; source 09]
Can the repository first certify the entire diamond example---semantics,
rank uniqueness, affine compiler, 133-variable quadratic, and exact
seven-zero count---and then replace its finite domain by an abstract
graph theorem without changing the interfaces?
\end{question}
This is a concrete integration target with a small enough independent
reference model to expose off-by-one comparisons, blank-site ranks,
seed conventions, and missing exterior terminality checks.

\wtag{} Compare \cref{cdc:q:verified}.

\subsection{Conclusion}
There are two different ways in which an arithmetic certificate can be
simple. It can be low-degree for each finite spatial instance, or it can
have one fixed finite coordinate list for every execution size. The
first does not imply the second.

For irreversible nonnegative self-assembly, earliest-arrival ranks make
finite producibility order-free. Two neighboring rank cuts suffice, and
unique-slack affine gadgets yield an explicit convex quadratic with one
natural zero per labelled assembly. The same correspondence survives a
careful whole-grid terminality test.

For fixed-arity representations subject to joint real-orthant
nonnegativity, degree at most three has an exact arithmetic limitation:
all projected natural zero sets are semilinear. Every semilinear set
already has a single-fold quadratic representation, while degree four reaches all
computably enumerable sets. This answers the precise degree question,
explains why the local compiler cannot itself be a cubic universal
compression, and provides two well-separated formalization targets for
ProveIt: canonical finite objects on the one hand, and a sharp
Presburger-versus-MRDP distinction on the other.


\part{Priority repetition: pumping bounds, program-uniform certificates and periodic tails}\label{cdc:part:pumping}

\paragraph{Source and scope.} \wtag{} This Part is manuscript~10, ``Sharp Pumping Bounds and Canonical Diophantine Certificates for Priority Arithmetic Computation'' (batch~62, manuscript~04; archive \path{ProveIt_Priority_Pumping_Diophantine.zip}, inner directory \path{priority_fractran_research}; shipped files prefixed \path{10-priority-pumping-}; labels \texttt{cdc:pf:}). It prints the manuscript's Sections 2--14 in their own order: ordered arithmetic computation and the exact FRACTRAN embedding; the priority-sensitive interval checker (\cref{cdc:pf:thm:interval}); least seeds and the exact repetition capacity (\cref{cdc:pf:thm:capacity}); the sharp pumping bound (\cref{cdc:pf:thm:pumping,cdc:pf:thm:sharp}); a canonical quartic uniform in the program entries (\cref{cdc:pf:thm:quartic}); variants and flat composition (\cref{cdc:pf:cor:flat}); infinite periodic tails (\cref{cdc:pf:thm:infinite}); computably enumerable completeness of eventual periodicity (\cref{cdc:pf:thm:ep}); affine macro certificates (\cref{cdc:pf:thm:affine}); validation; the formalization roadmap; the ten research questions; and the conclusion. Its three appendices follow. Its title, abstract, status statement and introduction are in \cref{cdc:sec:ms10}; the conventions of this Part are \cref{cdc:conv:b62-10}.

\paragraph{Relation to the other Parts.} \wtag{} Manuscript~10 inspected ProveIt at \texttt{4e128356d}, before this report existed, and does not cite it. Its central object is Part~III's: a fixed word repeated $k$ times, with $k$ a parameter and single-fold witnesses. It adds what Part~III's guarded translations lack, first-enabled-rule priority, under which an earlier rule must be \emph{disabled}, so that interior collision windows appear (\cref{cdc:pf:ex:interior}). For a fixed program the block relation $\Bvalid_{\mathcal P,w}(x,k,y)$ is an instance of Part~IV's run relation, and a single-fold quartic for it already follows from \cref{cdc:pt:thm:acceleration}; the priority-free fixed-word power is \cref{cdc:ct:prop:word-power}. The new content is uniformity in the program entries (they are free inputs of one polynomial), the exact capacity formula, the sharp threshold $2H+1$, polynomial witness height, and the theory of infinite tails, eventual periodicity and affine macros. Part~VII's FRACTRAN certificate (\cref{cdc:wf:thm:fractran}) certifies a bounded raw-integer run step by step; this Part accelerates a prescribed repeated word on exponent vectors, with size independent of the repetition count, and leaves the raw-integer interface open (its question on direct raw-integer interfaces). The flat-schema corollary partly answers the question on restricted unbounded classes (\cref{cdc:q:restricted}), and fixed-word acceleration with a single-fold certificate partly answers the question on substrate interfaces (\cref{cdc:q:interfaces}); see the notes there. The results on eventual periodicity and affine macros are nontermination certificates, the $\Sigma^0_1$ fragment of the recurrence and liveness hierarchy of the neighbouring report \emph{liveness-beyond-halting}; they stay here with the pumping theory they use.

\paragraph{Setting and hypotheses.} \wtag{} An ordered multiset program on $\N^d$ fires its first enabled rule; reduced FRACTRAN embeds by prime valuations. The instruction word $w$ and the dimensions $m,d$ are compiler data, while the program entries, the seed, the repetition count and the endpoint are free inputs of one polynomial. Neither universality nor a universal single-fold theorem is claimed.
